As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

By The Mercury News/East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/the-mercury-newseast-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 17, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 11:22 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.

Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

Very helpful. The Mercury News endorsement (YES) provides the strongest counterargument: the perverse incentive where government agencies route special taxes through "citizen initiatives" (paid for by unions/contractors) to bypass the two-thirds requirement — e.g., Measure RTM (regional transit sales tax, MTC could have placed it but then it would need two-thirds), Oakland Measure E. This is a real, documented abuse of the initiative process: "sham initiatives" run by government officials.

Also SF Prop G (2018 commercial rent tax for childcare) was literally engineered by the Board of Supervisors as a "citizen initiative" to avoid two-thirds — a clear case of officials gaming the system.

Now, let me get more on:
1. The KQED articles — "Prop. 43 would make it harder to raise local taxes. Can it pass?" and "Why opponents of Prop. 43 say it would cripple local funding."
2. The "manufactured initiative" problem in detail.
3. Any analysis of the ad valorem provision (b) — what it actually does. Important because it's undisclosed in the ballot summary. Let me check the WeHo council report which opposed it, and possibly legal analysis.
4. League of Women Voters recommendation.
5. The Chris Hoene op-ed (former California League of Cities) opposing.

Let me also check whether there's a "sham initiative" problem that the LAO / courts recognized — the San Diego hotel tax case where officials ran an initiative to bypass two-thirds. That's a strong pro-43 point.

Let me fetch KQED articles and the WeHo report.

Why Opponents of Prop. 43 Say It Would Cripple Local Funding
Opponents of Proposition 43 warn that requiring a two-thirds vote for citizen-led special taxes would choke off local revenue as federal funding dries up.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated 5:32 pm PT
Scott Shafer (https://www.kqed.org/author/scottshafer) Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA- MAY 5: In this photo illustration, an official voter information guide mailed to a Southern California resident, ahead of a state primary election, photographed May 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo Illustration by Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would raise the requirement for increasing special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens. Right now it takes a simple majority to pass those taxes, but Prop. 43 would require a two-thirds vote.
The initiative is supported by business groups and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Meanwhile, unions and the California League of Cities say Prop. 43 would cripple their ability to raise critical revenue at a time when the federal government is slashing funding to state and local governments.
Scott and Marisa talk to the No on 43 campaign’s Bill Barnes, who is director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California. Marisa previously discussed the Yes campaign with Jon Coupal (https://www.kqed.org/news/12095893/prop-43-would-make-it-harder-to-raise-local-taxes-can-it-pass), president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
Don’t forget to use KQED’s voter guide (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide) when filling out your ballot!
Plus, check out Political Breakdown’s weekly newsletter (https://www.kqed.org/newsletters/political-breakdown), delivered straight to your inbox.

CITY COUNCIL AUGUST 31, 2026
CONSENT CALENDAR
SUBJECT: CITY OF WEST HOLLYWOOD POSITIONS ON STATEWIDE
BALLOT INITIATIVES
PREPARED BY: CITY MANAGER'S DEPARTMENT
Jackie Rocco, City Manager
Andi Lovano, Assistant to the City Manager
Hernan Molina, Governmental Affairs Liaison
______________________________________________________________________
STATEMENT ON THE SUBJECT:
The City Council will consider adopting positions on different statewide ballot initiatives.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 1: THE VETERANS AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING
BOND ACT OF 2026.
2. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 3: RENEW STATE INCOME TAX INCREASE FOR
EDUCATION FUNDING.
3. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 37: SECOND MORTGAGE HOMEBUYER
PROGRAM AND REVENUE BOND.
4. OPPOSE PROPOSITION 43: TWO-THIRDS VOTE REQUIREMENT FOR LOCAL
SPECIAL TAX INITIATIVES AND PROPERTY TAX INITIATIVE PROHIBITION
AMENDMENT.
5. Direct staff to publish the City Council’s adopted positions on the City’s web page.
BACKGROUND / ANALYSIS:
Since the City’s incorporation in November 1984, different City Councils have weighed in
on different statewide ballot initiatives and local measures that directly or indirectly could
have a negative or positive impact on the City and its citizenry. This year, as citizens
AGENDA ITEM B.6.
Page 2 of 8
prepare to participate in the November 3, 2026, election, they will be asked to approve or
reject up to 14 statewide ballot initiatives. Staff reviewed the initiatives qualified to appear
on the November 3 ballot and determined that a few of them are relevant to the City. In
addition, some of the propositions analyzed are proposing modifications to previously
approved propositions, which were supported by the City Council. Such is the case of
Proposition 3, which seeks to make permanent the tax on very high-income earners,
which was first proposed in 2012 and then amended in 2016.
The following analyses and recommendations are presented to the City Council taking
into account the potential impact of these ballot initiatives on the City as a municipal
agency and the residents of West Hollywood. In addition, the recommendations are based
on the City’s previously adopted policies and the 2025-2026 legislative priorities.
PROPOSITION 1: THE VETERANS AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING BOND ACT OF
2026
Type of initiative: Legislatively referred. Senate Bill (SB) 417 was introduced by Senate
President Pro Tempore, Monique Limon, D-Santa Barbara, and approved by Governor
Newsom on June 25, 2026.
Proposition 1 will authorize the state to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to fund income-
qualified housing programs. More specifically, the proceeds will be assigned as follows:
• $10 billion would be used to finance programs to fund affordable rental housing
and home ownership programs, including, among others, the Multifamily Housing
Program, the CalHome Program, and the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing
Grant Program.
• $1,25 billion would be used to provide additional funding for the above-described
program for farm, home, and mobile home purchase assistance for veterans.
Over the last twenty years, the state of California has struggled to meet demand for safe
and affordable housing in the state. Different, reputable organizations estimate the
housing shortage to range from 800,000 to more than 3 million housing units. Affordability
itself is a major concern not only for prospective buyers but also for renters. Over the last
twenty years, rents skyrocketed while incomes remained largely flat. The elimination of
Page 3 of 8
Community Redevelopment Agencies (CRA) by the state in 2011, has worsened the crisis
of housing affordability by drastically reducing funding to build affordable.
Since its incorporation, the City of West Hollywood, which was founded by a coalition of
concerned seniors, renters, LGBTQ+ people, people living with disabilities, and other
groups, pursued and instituted progressive housing/tenancy policies to stabilize the local
housing market. Right upon the time of incorporation, one of the first actions of the newly
installed City Council was to adopt a Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO), which brought
much needed certainty to thousands of renters, many of whom were seniors living on
fixed incomes. The Council also adopted the Inclusionary Zoning Ordinance, requiring
that new housing developments include affordable housing units for renters on different
income levels.
The City Council’s adopted legislative priorities that were first officially adopted in the early
2000s, and were informed by past Council actions, include policy priorities that align with
the intent of Proposition 1, and these are:
H&HS 16: Support legislation that will increase state and federal funding for the care of
injured and disabled veterans of all ages.
H&HS 17: Support legislation that addresses the need for housing and supportive
services, e.g., health, mental health and substance use disorder services and social
services for the City’s unhoused population. This includes the expansion of MediCal to
cover ancillary support services.
H&RS 1: Support legislation and funding that encourages the production of a diverse
housing stock in new developments to address the needs of all socio-economic segments
of the community.
SB 3: Support a state budget that includes funding for affordable housing for very low,
low, moderate-income families.
Recommendation: Based on the above considerations and previously adopted policies,
staff recommend the City Council adopt a support position on Proposition 1.
Page 4 of 8
PROPOSITION 3: RENEW STATE INCOME TAX INCREASE FOR EDUCATION
FUNDING
Type of initiative: Initiated constitutional amendment. This proposal, which aims to amend
the state constitution, was originated by citizens who gathered signatures from registered
voters to qualify the initiative to be placed on the ballot.
Proposition 3 proposes amending the state constitution to indefinitely extend the top
marginal tax rates set to expire in 2031 on single filers earning at least $361,000 or joint
filers earning at least $721,000, with 89% of revenue allocated to K–12 schools and 11%
to community colleges.
In 2012, California voters approved Proposition 30, which imposed a temporary tax on
high income earners to fund education. Then in 2016, the tax was extended when voters
approved Proposition 55. As approved, neither Prop 30 nor Prop 55 included mechanisms
to take into account the effects of inflation. Proposition 3 increases the threshold and ties
it to inflation. Proposition 3 is sponsored by the California Teachers Association (CTA).
The City of West Hollywood has long advocated for adequate funding levels for education
to ensure that teachers are adequately remunerated and school infrastructure is in par
with the delivery of high-quality education. In addition, the City has supported a variety of
legislative initiatives aimed at protecting all students from harassment and discrimination.
The City’s 2025-2026 legislative priorities include the following policy priorities:
ED 3: Support legislation that will provide funding for improvements to public schools that
directly benefit and enhance students’ education, including curriculum, instructional
materials, and infrastructure needs.
ED 5: Support legislation and funding for the restoration and/or enhancement of arts
programs in public schools.
SB 4: Support a state budget that funds food and nutrition, and education support
programs for low-income families.
Recommendation: Based on the above, staff recommend the City Council support
Proposition 3.
Page 5 of 8
PROPOSITION 37: SECOND MORTGAGE HOMEBUYER PROGRAM AND REVENUE
BOND
Type of initiative: Initiated state statue. This proposal, which aims to amend existing laws,
was originated by citizens who gathered signatures from registered voters to qualify the
initiative to be placed on the ballot.
Proposition 37 will authorize the creation of a second mortgage program to be
administered by California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) and funded by the
proceeds of state revenue bonds in an amount not to exceed $25 billion. The program
aims to assist working families who can make monthly mortgage payments but may not
have enough money for the usual downpayment of fifteen percent. The program will offer
a second mortgage of up to 17 percent of a home’s sales price to people meeting the
following requirements:
• Applicants must be California residents of at least one year,
• Have earnings at or below 200% of the area median income for a similar-sized
family in the county or city where the home is located, and
• Provide a down payment of at least 3% of the purchase price — on qualifying
homes.
As mentioned above, California is not only facing a housing crisis due to not building
enough but is also facing an affordability crisis. More and more Americans are being
prevented from owning their homes. This middle-class homeownership loan program
would help working families and individuals bridge the gap between incomes and home
prices by making it easier to obtain funds to pay for the downpayment for a home.
Like Proposition 1, this ballot initiative aligns with the City’s legislative priorities and the
progressive housing policies different City Councils have supported over the years.
Recommendation: Based on the above, staff recommend the City Council support
Proposition 37.
Page 6 of 8
PROPOSITION 43: TWO-THIRDS VOTE REQUIREMENT FOR LOCAL SPECIAL TAX
INITIATIVES AND PROPERTY TAX INITIATIVE PROHIBITION AMENDMENT
Type of initiative: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment. Assembly
Constitutional Amendment (ACA) 22 Local taxes: limitation, was introduced by
Assembymember Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland and approved by Governor Newsom on June
25, 2026.
Proposition 43 is the result of a compromise between the Governor’s office and the
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which was sponsoring a ballot initiative that would
have made increased the threshold for passage of local tax measures from a simple
majority to a super majority of 66.7% of votes, retroactively. The retroactive nature of the
initiative would have resulted in measures passed with a simple majority since 2017 to be
voided.
As approved on June 25, the proposition will require, starting January 1, 2027, the
approval of a local tax measure with a two-thirds vote. In addition, no local government
or the electorate may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as prescribed by
the California constitution.
This proposition will make it harder for local governments to pass new tax measures. Said
taxes have helped cities to remain fiscally viable and at the same time, maintain high
quality services to their residents.
Over the years, the City of West Hollywood worked to secure voter approval of tax
measures to pay for augmented human services programs aimed at assisting unhoused
individuals. For instance, in 2020, the City included Measure E on the November 3, 2020,
ballot, which enacted a ¾ cent local sales tax to address the COVID-19 shortfall, and
maintain the services West Hollywood residents have indicated are important, such as
addressing homelessness, expanding health and mental health services, retaining local
businesses and jobs, keeping public areas clean and safe, maintaining HIV and AIDS
health services, supporting disaster preparedness, etc. Measure E received 73% of the
total votes cast.
In 2024, and in response to the County’s tax Measure A that repealed Measure H and
Page 7 of 8
increased the County’s sales tax was approved by the voters. At the same time, the City
asked voters to consider supporting Measure WH, Pre-Authorization of a Sales Tax
Measure, which gave preauthorization to the City to redirect 0.25% of the local sales tax
if Measure H sunsets or is repealed. Measure WH passed with overwhelming support of
West Hollywood voters (82%).
Recommendation:
Even though West Hollywood voters have supported the above-mentioned local
measures well above the proposed 66.7% of the votes cast, Proposition 43 would be a
hindrance to many local governments, which rely on limited sources of revenues for the
delivery of services. Therefore, the City Council is recommended to oppose this initiative.
CONFORMANCE WITH VISION 2020 AND THE GOALS OF THE WEST HOLLYWOOD
GENERAL PLAN:
This item is consistent with the Primary Strategic Goal(s) (PSG) and/or Ongoing Strategic
Program(s) (OSP) of:
• OSP-12: Actively Participate in Regional Issues.
In addition, this item is compliant with the following goal(s) of the West Hollywood General
Plan:
• G-1: Ensure that the community is active and engaged in the decision-making process.
EVALUATION PROCESSES:
N/A
ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND HEALTH:
N/A
COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT:
The City’s Communications Department commonly shares City-related information with
the community at large about via its established communication channels, including
Page 8 of 8
posting of information about the City Council’s actions on the City’s web page
www.weho.org

CITY MANAGER'S DEPARTMENT / CITY MANAGER OFFICE

None.

Why Opponents of Prop. 43 Say It Would Cripple Local Funding
Opponents of Proposition 43 warn that requiring a two-thirds vote for citizen-led special taxes would choke off local revenue as federal funding dries up.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated 5:32 pm PT
Scott Shafer (https://www.kqed.org/author/scottshafer) Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA- MAY 5: In this photo illustration, an official voter information guide mailed to a Southern California resident, ahead of a state primary election, photographed May 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo Illustration by Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would raise the requirement for increasing special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens. Right now it takes a simple majority to pass those taxes, but Prop. 43 would require a two-thirds vote.
The initiative is supported by business groups and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Meanwhile, unions and the California League of Cities say Prop. 43 would cripple their ability to raise critical revenue at a time when the federal government is slashing funding to state and local governments.
Scott and Marisa talk to the No on 43 campaign’s Bill Barnes, who is director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California. Marisa previously discussed the Yes campaign with Jon Coupal (https://www.kqed.org/news/12095893/prop-43-would-make-it-harder-to-raise-local-taxes-can-it-pass), president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

CITY COUNCIL AUGUST 31, 2026
CONSENT CALENDAR
SUBJECT: CITY OF WEST HOLLYWOOD POSITIONS ON STATEWIDE
BALLOT INITIATIVES
PREPARED BY: CITY MANAGER'S DEPARTMENT
Jackie Rocco, City Manager
Andi Lovano, Assistant to the City Manager
Hernan Molina, Governmental Affairs Liaison
______________________________________________________________________
STATEMENT ON THE SUBJECT:
The City Council will consider adopting positions on different statewide ballot initiatives.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 1: THE VETERANS AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING
BOND ACT OF 2026.
2. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 3: RENEW STATE INCOME TAX INCREASE FOR
EDUCATION FUNDING.
3. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 37: SECOND MORTGAGE HOMEBUYER
PROGRAM AND REVENUE BOND.
4. OPPOSE PROPOSITION 43: TWO-THIRDS VOTE REQUIREMENT FOR LOCAL
SPECIAL TAX INITIATIVES AND PROPERTY TAX INITIATIVE PROHIBITION
AMENDMENT.
5. Direct staff to publish the City Council’s adopted positions on the City’s web page.
BACKGROUND / ANALYSIS:
Since the City’s incorporation in November 1984, different City Councils have weighed in
on different statewide ballot initiatives and local measures that directly or indirectly could
have a negative or positive impact on the City and its citizenry. This year, as citizens
AGENDA ITEM B.6.
Page 2 of 8
prepare to participate in the November 3, 2026, election, they will be asked to approve or
reject up to 14 statewide ballot initiatives. Staff reviewed the initiatives qualified to appear
on the November 3 ballot and determined that a few of them are relevant to the City. In
addition, some of the propositions analyzed are proposing modifications to previously
approved propositions, which were supported by the City Council. Such is the case of
Proposition 3, which seeks to make permanent the tax on very high-income earners,
which was first proposed in 2012 and then amended in 2016.
The following analyses and recommendations are presented to the City Council taking
into account the potential impact of these ballot initiatives on the City as a municipal
agency and the residents of West Hollywood. In addition, the recommendations are based
on the City’s previously adopted policies and the 2025-2026 legislative priorities.
PROPOSITION 1: THE VETERANS AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING BOND ACT OF
2026
Type of initiative: Legislatively referred. Senate Bill (SB) 417 was introduced by Senate
President Pro Tempore, Monique Limon, D-Santa Barbara, and approved by Governor
Newsom on June 25, 2026.
Proposition 1 will authorize the state to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to fund income-
qualified housing programs. More specifically, the proceeds will be assigned as follows:
• $10 billion would be used to finance programs to fund affordable rental housing
and home ownership programs, including, among others, the Multifamily Housing
Program, the CalHome Program, and the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing
Grant Program.
• $1,25 billion would be used to provide additional funding for the above-described
program for farm, home, and mobile home purchase assistance for veterans.
Over the last twenty years, the state of California has struggled to meet demand for safe
and affordable housing in the state. Different, reputable organizations estimate the
housing shortage to range from 800,000 to more than 3 million housing units. Affordability
itself is a major concern not only for prospective buyers but also for renters. Over the last
twenty years, rents skyrocketed while incomes remained largely flat. The elimination of
Page 3 of 8
Community Redevelopment Agencies (CRA) by the state in 2011, has worsened the crisis
of housing affordability by drastically reducing funding to build affordable.
Since its incorporation, the City of West Hollywood, which was founded by a coalition of
concerned seniors, renters, LGBTQ+ people, people living with disabilities, and other
groups, pursued and instituted progressive housing/tenancy policies to stabilize the local
housing market. Right upon the time of incorporation, one of the first actions of the newly
installed City Council was to adopt a Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO), which brought
much needed certainty to thousands of renters, many of whom were seniors living on
fixed incomes. The Council also adopted the Inclusionary Zoning Ordinance, requiring
that new housing developments include affordable housing units for renters on different
income levels.
The City Council’s adopted legislative priorities that were first officially adopted in the early
2000s, and were informed by past Council actions, include policy priorities that align with
the intent of Proposition 1, and these are:
H&HS 16: Support legislation that will increase state and federal funding for the care of
injured and disabled veterans of all ages.
H&HS 17: Support legislation that addresses the need for housing and supportive
services, e.g., health, mental health and substance use disorder services and social
services for the City’s unhoused population. This includes the expansion of MediCal to
cover ancillary support services.
H&RS 1: Support legislation and funding that encourages the production of a diverse
housing stock in new developments to address the needs of all socio-economic segments
of the community.
SB 3: Support a state budget that includes funding for affordable housing for very low,
low, moderate-income families.
Recommendation: Based on the above considerations and previously adopted policies,
staff recommend the City Council adopt a support position on Proposition 1.
Page 4 of 8
PROPOSITION 3: RENEW STATE INCOME TAX INCREASE FOR EDUCATION
FUNDING
Type of initiative: Initiated constitutional amendment. This proposal, which aims to amend
the state constitution, was originated by citizens who gathered signatures from registered
voters to qualify the initiative to be placed on the ballot.
Proposition 3 proposes amending the state constitution to indefinitely extend the top
marginal tax rates set to expire in 2031 on single filers earning at least $361,000 or joint
filers earning at least $721,000, with 89% of revenue allocated to K–12 schools and 11%
to community colleges.
In 2012, California voters approved Proposition 30, which imposed a temporary tax on
high income earners to fund education. Then in 2016, the tax was extended when voters
approved Proposition 55. As approved, neither Prop 30 nor Prop 55 included mechanisms
to take into account the effects of inflation. Proposition 3 increases the threshold and ties
it to inflation. Proposition 3 is sponsored by the California Teachers Association (CTA).
The City of West Hollywood has long advocated for adequate funding levels for education
to ensure that teachers are adequately remunerated and school infrastructure is in par
with the delivery of high-quality education. In addition, the City has supported a variety of
legislative initiatives aimed at protecting all students from harassment and discrimination.
The City’s 2025-2026 legislative priorities include the following policy priorities:
ED 3: Support legislation that will provide funding for improvements to public schools that
directly benefit and enhance students’ education, including curriculum, instructional
materials, and infrastructure needs.
ED 5: Support legislation and funding for the restoration and/or enhancement of arts
programs in public schools.
SB 4: Support a state budget that funds food and nutrition, and education support
programs for low-income families.
Recommendation: Based on the above, staff recommend the City Council support
Proposition 3.
Page 5 of 8
PROPOSITION 37: SECOND MORTGAGE HOMEBUYER PROGRAM AND REVENUE
BOND
Type of initiative: Initiated state statue. This proposal, which aims to amend existing laws,
was originated by citizens who gathered signatures from registered voters to qualify the
initiative to be placed on the ballot.
Proposition 37 will authorize the creation of a second mortgage program to be
administered by California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) and funded by the
proceeds of state revenue bonds in an amount not to exceed $25 billion. The program
aims to assist working families who can make monthly mortgage payments but may not
have enough money for the usual downpayment of fifteen percent. The program will offer
a second mortgage of up to 17 percent of a home’s sales price to people meeting the
following requirements:
• Applicants must be California residents of at least one year,
• Have earnings at or below 200% of the area median income for a similar-sized
family in the county or city where the home is located, and
• Provide a down payment of at least 3% of the purchase price — on qualifying
homes.
As mentioned above, California is not only facing a housing crisis due to not building
enough but is also facing an affordability crisis. More and more Americans are being
prevented from owning their homes. This middle-class homeownership loan program
would help working families and individuals bridge the gap between incomes and home
prices by making it easier to obtain funds to pay for the downpayment for a home.
Like Proposition 1, this ballot initiative aligns with the City’s legislative priorities and the
progressive housing policies different City Councils have supported over the years.
Recommendation: Based on the above, staff recommend the City Council support
Proposition 37.
Page 6 of 8
PROPOSITION 43: TWO-THIRDS VOTE REQUIREMENT FOR LOCAL SPECIAL TAX
INITIATIVES AND PROPERTY TAX INITIATIVE PROHIBITION AMENDMENT
Type of initiative: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment. Assembly
Constitutional Amendment (ACA) 22 Local taxes: limitation, was introduced by
Assembymember Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland and approved by Governor Newsom on June
25, 2026.
Proposition 43 is the result of a compromise between the Governor’s office and the
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which was sponsoring a ballot initiative that would
have made increased the threshold for passage of local tax measures from a simple
majority to a super majority of 66.7% of votes, retroactively. The retroactive nature of the
initiative would have resulted in measures passed with a simple majority since 2017 to be
voided.
As approved on June 25, the proposition will require, starting January 1, 2027, the
approval of a local tax measure with a two-thirds vote. In addition, no local government
or the electorate may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as prescribed by
the California constitution.
This proposition will make it harder for local governments to pass new tax measures. Said
taxes have helped cities to remain fiscally viable and at the same time, maintain high
quality services to their residents.
Over the years, the City of West Hollywood worked to secure voter approval of tax
measures to pay for augmented human services programs aimed at assisting unhoused
individuals. For instance, in 2020, the City included Measure E on the November 3, 2020,
ballot, which enacted a ¾ cent local sales tax to address the COVID-19 shortfall, and
maintain the services West Hollywood residents have indicated are important, such as
addressing homelessness, expanding health and mental health services, retaining local
businesses and jobs, keeping public areas clean and safe, maintaining HIV and AIDS
health services, supporting disaster preparedness, etc. Measure E received 73% of the
total votes cast.
In 2024, and in response to the County’s tax Measure A that repealed Measure H and
Page 7 of 8
increased the County’s sales tax was approved by the voters. At the same time, the City
asked voters to consider supporting Measure WH, Pre-Authorization of a Sales Tax
Measure, which gave preauthorization to the City to redirect 0.25% of the local sales tax
if Measure H sunsets or is repealed. Measure WH passed with overwhelming support of
West Hollywood voters (82%).
Recommendation:
Even though West Hollywood voters have supported the above-mentioned local
measures well above the proposed 66.7% of the votes cast, Proposition 43 would be a
hindrance to many local governments, which rely on limited sources of revenues for the
delivery of services. Therefore, the City Council is recommended to oppose this initiative.

SUBJECT: CITY OF WEST HOLLYWOOD POSITIONS ON STATEWIDE

PREPARED BY: CITY MANAGER'S DEPARTMENT
Jackie Rocco, City Manager

STATEMENT ON THE SUBJECT:
The City Council will consider adopting positions on different statewide ballot initiatives.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 1: THE VETERANS AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING
BOND ACT OF 2026.
2. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 3: RENEW STATE INCOME TAX INCREASE FOR
EDUCATION FUNDING.
3. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 37: SECOND MORTGAGE HOMEBUYER
PROGRAM AND REVENUE BOND.
4. OPPOSE PROPOSITION 43: TWO-THIRDS VOTE REQUIREMENT FOR LOCAL
SPECIAL TAX INITIATIVES AND PROPERTY TAX INITIATIVE PROHIBITION
AMENDMENT.
5. Direct staff to publish the City Council’s adopted positions on the City’s web page.
BACKGROUND / ANALYSIS:
Since the City’s incorporation in November 1984, different City Councils have weighed in
on different statewide ballot initiatives and local measures that directly or indirectly could
have a negative or positive impact on the City and its citizenry. This year, as citizens
AGENDA ITEM B.6.
Page 2 of 8
prepare to participate in the November 3, 2026, election, they will be asked to approve or
reject up to 14 statewide ballot initiatives. Staff reviewed the initiatives qualified to appear
on the November 3 ballot and determined that a few of them are relevant to the City. In
addition, some of the propositions analyzed are proposing modifications to previously
approved propositions, which were supported by the City Council. Such is the case of
Proposition 3, which seeks to make permanent the tax on very high-income earners,
which was first proposed in 2012 and then amended in 2016.
The following analyses and recommendations are presented to the City Council taking
into account the potential impact of these ballot initiatives on the City as a municipal
agency and the residents of West Hollywood. In addition, the recommendations are based
on the City’s previously adopted policies and the 2025-2026 legislative priorities.
PROPOSITION 1: THE VETERANS AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING BOND ACT OF
2026
Type of initiative: Legislatively referred. Senate Bill (SB) 417 was introduced by Senate
President Pro Tempore, Monique Limon, D-Santa Barbara, and approved by Governor
Newsom on June 25, 2026.
Proposition 1 will authorize the state to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to fund income-
qualified housing programs. More specifically, the proceeds will be assigned as follows:
• $10 billion would be used to finance programs to fund affordable rental housing
and home ownership programs, including, among others, the Multifamily Housing
Program, the CalHome Program, and the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing
Grant Program.
• $1,25 billion would be used to provide additional funding for the above-described
program for farm, home, and mobile home purchase assistance for veterans.
Over the last twenty years, the state of California has struggled to meet demand for safe
and affordable housing in the state. Different, reputable organizations estimate the
housing shortage to range from 800,000 to more than 3 million housing units. Affordability
itself is a major concern not only for prospective buyers but also for renters. Over the last
twenty years, rents skyrocketed while incomes remained largely flat. The elimination of
Page 3 of 8
Community Redevelopment Agencies (CRA) by the state in 2011, has worsened the crisis
of housing affordability by drastically reducing funding to build affordable.
Since its incorporation, the City of West Hollywood, which was founded by a coalition of
concerned seniors, renters, LGBTQ+ people, people living with disabilities, and other
groups, pursued and instituted progressive housing/tenancy policies to stabilize the local
housing market. Right upon the time of incorporation, one of the first actions of the newly
installed City Council was to adopt a Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO), which brought
much needed certainty to thousands of renters, many of whom were seniors living on
fixed incomes. The Council also adopted the Inclusionary Zoning Ordinance, requiring
that new housing developments include affordable housing units for renters on different
income levels.
The City Council’s adopted legislative priorities that were first officially adopted in the early
2000s, and were informed by past Council actions, include policy priorities that align with
the intent of Proposition 1, and these are:
H&HS 16: Support legislation that will increase state and federal funding for the care of
injured and disabled veterans of all ages.
H&HS 17: Support legislation that addresses the need for housing and supportive
services, e.g., health, mental health and substance use disorder services and social
services for the City’s unhoused population. This includes the expansion of MediCal to
cover ancillary support services.
H&RS 1: Support legislation and funding that encourages the production of a diverse
housing stock in new developments to address the needs of all socio-economic segments
of the community.
SB 3: Support a state budget that includes funding for affordable housing for very low,
low, moderate-income families.
Recommendation: Based on the above considerations and previously adopted policies,
staff recommend the City Council adopt a support position on Proposition 1.
Page 4 of 8
PROPOSITION 3: RENEW STATE INCOME TAX INCREASE FOR EDUCATION
FUNDING
Type of initiative: Initiated constitutional amendment. This proposal, which aims to amend
the state constitution, was originated by citizens who gathered signatures from registered
voters to qualify the initiative to be placed on the ballot.
Proposition 3 proposes amending the state constitution to indefinitely extend the top
marginal tax rates set to expire in 2031 on single filers earning at least $361,000 or joint
filers earning at least $721,000, with 89% of revenue allocated to K–12 schools and 11%
to community colleges.
In 2012, California voters approved Proposition 30, which imposed a temporary tax on
high income earners to fund education. Then in 2016, the tax was extended when voters
approved Proposition 55. As approved, neither Prop 30 nor Prop 55 included mechanisms

it to inflation. Proposition 3 is sponsored by the California Teachers Association (CTA).
The City of West Hollywood has long advocated for adequate funding levels for education
to ensure that teachers are adequately remunerated and school infrastructure is in par
with the delivery of high-quality education. In addition, the City has supported a variety of
legislative initiatives aimed at protecting all students from harassment and discrimination.
The City’s 2025-2026 legislative priorities include the following policy priorities:
ED 3: Support legislation that will provide funding for improvements to public schools that
directly benefit and enhance students’ education, including curriculum, instructional
materials, and infrastructure needs.
ED 5: Support legislation and funding for the restoration and/or enhancement of arts
programs in public schools.
SB 4: Support a state budget that funds food and nutrition, and education support
programs for low-income families.

Proposition 3.

Very helpful. The Mercury News endorsement (YES) provides the strongest counterargument: the perverse incentive where government agencies route special taxes through "citizen initiatives" (paid for by unions/contractors) to bypass the two-thirds requirement — e.g., Measure RTM (regional transit sales tax, MTC could have placed it but then it would need two-thirds), Oakland Measure E. This is a real, documented abuse of the initiative process: "sham initiatives" run by government officials.

Also SF Prop G (2018 commercial rent tax for childcare) was literally engineered by the Board of Supervisors as a "citizen initiative" to avoid two-thirds — a clear case of officials gaming the system.

Now, let me get more on:
1. The KQED articles — "Prop. 43 would make it harder to raise local taxes. Can it pass?" and "Why opponents of Prop. 43 say it would cripple local funding."
2. The "manufactured initiative" problem in detail.
3. Any analysis of the ad valorem provision (b) — what it actually does. Important because it's undisclosed in the ballot summary. Let me check the WeHo council report which opposed it, and possibly legal analysis.
4. League of Women Voters recommendation.
5. The Chris Hoene op-ed (former California League of Cities) opposing.

Let me also check whether there's a "sham initiative" problem that the LAO / courts recognized — the San Diego hotel tax case where officials ran an initiative to bypass two-thirds. That's a strong pro-43 point.

Let me fetch KQED articles and the WeHo report.

Why Opponents of Prop. 43 Say It Would Cripple Local Funding
Opponents of Proposition 43 warn that requiring a two-thirds vote for citizen-led special taxes would choke off local revenue as federal funding dries up.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated 5:32 pm PT
Scott Shafer (https://www.kqed.org/author/scottshafer) Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA- MAY 5: In this photo illustration, an official voter information guide mailed to a Southern California resident, ahead of a state primary election, photographed May 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo Illustration by Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would raise the requirement for increasing special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens. Right now it takes a simple majority to pass those taxes, but Prop. 43 would require a two-thirds vote.
The initiative is supported by business groups and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Meanwhile, unions and the California League of Cities say Prop. 43 would cripple their ability to raise critical revenue at a time when the federal government is slashing funding to state and local governments.
Scott and Marisa talk to the No on 43 campaign’s Bill Barnes, who is director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California. Marisa previously discussed the Yes campaign with Jon Coupal (https://www.kqed.org/news/12095893/prop-43-would-make-it-harder-to-raise-local-taxes-can-it-pass), president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
Don’t forget to use KQED’s voter guide (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide) when filling out your ballot!
Plus, check out Political Breakdown’s weekly newsletter (https://www.kqed.org/newsletters/political-breakdown), delivered straight to your inbox.
