CITY COUNCIL AUGUST 31, 2026
CONSENT CALENDAR
SUBJECT: CITY OF WEST HOLLYWOOD POSITIONS ON STATEWIDE
BALLOT INITIATIVES
PREPARED BY: CITY MANAGER'S DEPARTMENT
Jackie Rocco, City Manager
Andi Lovano, Assistant to the City Manager
Hernan Molina, Governmental Affairs Liaison
______________________________________________________________________
STATEMENT ON THE SUBJECT:
The City Council will consider adopting positions on different statewide ballot initiatives.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 1: THE VETERANS AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING
BOND ACT OF 2026.
2. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 3: RENEW STATE INCOME TAX INCREASE FOR
EDUCATION FUNDING.
3. SUPPORT PROPOSITION 37: SECOND MORTGAGE HOMEBUYER
PROGRAM AND REVENUE BOND.
4. OPPOSE PROPOSITION 43: TWO-THIRDS VOTE REQUIREMENT FOR LOCAL
SPECIAL TAX INITIATIVES AND PROPERTY TAX INITIATIVE PROHIBITION
AMENDMENT.
5. Direct staff to publish the City Council’s adopted positions on the City’s web page.
BACKGROUND / ANALYSIS:
Since the City’s incorporation in November 1984, different City Councils have weighed in
on different statewide ballot initiatives and local measures that directly or indirectly could
have a negative or positive impact on the City and its citizenry. This year, as citizens
AGENDA ITEM B.6.
Page 2 of 8
prepare to participate in the November 3, 2026, election, they will be asked to approve or
reject up to 14 statewide ballot initiatives. Staff reviewed the initiatives qualified to appear
on the November 3 ballot and determined that a few of them are relevant to the City. In
addition, some of the propositions analyzed are proposing modifications to previously
approved propositions, which were supported by the City Council. Such is the case of
Proposition 3, which seeks to make permanent the tax on very high-income earners,
which was first proposed in 2012 and then amended in 2016.
The following analyses and recommendations are presented to the City Council taking
into account the potential impact of these ballot initiatives on the City as a municipal
agency and the residents of West Hollywood. In addition, the recommendations are based
on the City’s previously adopted policies and the 2025-2026 legislative priorities.
PROPOSITION 1: THE VETERANS AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING BOND ACT OF
2026
Type of initiative: Legislatively referred. Senate Bill (SB) 417 was introduced by Senate
President Pro Tempore, Monique Limon, D-Santa Barbara, and approved by Governor
Newsom on June 25, 2026.
Proposition 1 will authorize the state to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to fund income-
qualified housing programs. More specifically, the proceeds will be assigned as follows:
• $10 billion would be used to finance programs to fund affordable rental housing
and home ownership programs, including, among others, the Multifamily Housing
Program, the CalHome Program, and the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing
Grant Program.
• $1,25 billion would be used to provide additional funding for the above-described
program for farm, home, and mobile home purchase assistance for veterans.
Over the last twenty years, the state of California has struggled to meet demand for safe
and affordable housing in the state. Different, reputable organizations estimate the
housing shortage to range from 800,000 to more than 3 million housing units. Affordability
itself is a major concern not only for prospective buyers but also for renters. Over the last
twenty years, rents skyrocketed while incomes remained largely flat. The elimination of
Page 3 of 8
Community Redevelopment Agencies (CRA) by the state in 2011, has worsened the crisis
of housing affordability by drastically reducing funding to build affordable.
Since its incorporation, the City of West Hollywood, which was founded by a coalition of
concerned seniors, renters, LGBTQ+ people, people living with disabilities, and other
groups, pursued and instituted progressive housing/tenancy policies to stabilize the local
housing market. Right upon the time of incorporation, one of the first actions of the newly
installed City Council was to adopt a Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO), which brought
much needed certainty to thousands of renters, many of whom were seniors living on
fixed incomes. The Council also adopted the Inclusionary Zoning Ordinance, requiring
that new housing developments include affordable housing units for renters on different
income levels.
The City Council’s adopted legislative priorities that were first officially adopted in the early
2000s, and were informed by past Council actions, include policy priorities that align with
the intent of Proposition 1, and these are:
H&HS 16: Support legislation that will increase state and federal funding for the care of
injured and disabled veterans of all ages.
H&HS 17: Support legislation that addresses the need for housing and supportive
services, e.g., health, mental health and substance use disorder services and social
services for the City’s unhoused population. This includes the expansion of MediCal to
cover ancillary support services.
H&RS 1: Support legislation and funding that encourages the production of a diverse
housing stock in new developments to address the needs of all socio-economic segments
of the community.
SB 3: Support a state budget that includes funding for affordable housing for very low,
low, moderate-income families.
Recommendation: Based on the above considerations and previously adopted policies,
staff recommend the City Council adopt a support position on Proposition 1.
Page 4 of 8
PROPOSITION 3: RENEW STATE INCOME TAX INCREASE FOR EDUCATION
FUNDING
Type of initiative: Initiated constitutional amendment. This proposal, which aims to amend
the state constitution, was originated by citizens who gathered signatures from registered
voters to qualify the initiative to be placed on the ballot.
Proposition 3 proposes amending the state constitution to indefinitely extend the top
marginal tax rates set to expire in 2031 on single filers earning at least $361,000 or joint
filers earning at least $721,000, with 89% of revenue allocated to K–12 schools and 11%
to community colleges.
In 2012, California voters approved Proposition 30, which imposed a temporary tax on
high income earners to fund education. Then in 2016, the tax was extended when voters
approved Proposition 55. As approved, neither Prop 30 nor Prop 55 included mechanisms
to take into account the effects of inflation. Proposition 3 increases the threshold and ties
it to inflation. Proposition 3 is sponsored by the California Teachers Association (CTA).
The City of West Hollywood has long advocated for adequate funding levels for education
to ensure that teachers are adequately remunerated and school infrastructure is in par
with the delivery of high-quality education. In addition, the City has supported a variety of
legislative initiatives aimed at protecting all students from harassment and discrimination.
The City’s 2025-2026 legislative priorities include the following policy priorities:
ED 3: Support legislation that will provide funding for improvements to public schools that
directly benefit and enhance students’ education, including curriculum, instructional
materials, and infrastructure needs.
ED 5: Support legislation and funding for the restoration and/or enhancement of arts
programs in public schools.
SB 4: Support a state budget that funds food and nutrition, and education support
programs for low-income families.
Recommendation: Based on the above, staff recommend the City Council support
Proposition 3.
Page 5 of 8
PROPOSITION 37: SECOND MORTGAGE HOMEBUYER PROGRAM AND REVENUE
BOND
Type of initiative: Initiated state statue. This proposal, which aims to amend existing laws,
was originated by citizens who gathered signatures from registered voters to qualify the
initiative to be placed on the ballot.
Proposition 37 will authorize the creation of a second mortgage program to be
administered by California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) and funded by the
proceeds of state revenue bonds in an amount not to exceed $25 billion. The program
aims to assist working families who can make monthly mortgage payments but may not
have enough money for the usual downpayment of fifteen percent. The program will offer
a second mortgage of up to 17 percent of a home’s sales price to people meeting the
following requirements:
• Applicants must be California residents of at least one year,
• Have earnings at or below 200% of the area median income for a similar-sized
family in the county or city where the home is located, and
• Provide a down payment of at least 3% of the purchase price — on qualifying
homes.
As mentioned above, California is not only facing a housing crisis due to not building
enough but is also facing an affordability crisis. More and more Americans are being
prevented from owning their homes. This middle-class homeownership loan program
would help working families and individuals bridge the gap between incomes and home
prices by making it easier to obtain funds to pay for the downpayment for a home.
Like Proposition 1, this ballot initiative aligns with the City’s legislative priorities and the
progressive housing policies different City Councils have supported over the years.
Recommendation: Based on the above, staff recommend the City Council support
Proposition 37.
Page 6 of 8
PROPOSITION 43: TWO-THIRDS VOTE REQUIREMENT FOR LOCAL SPECIAL TAX
INITIATIVES AND PROPERTY TAX INITIATIVE PROHIBITION AMENDMENT
Type of initiative: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment. Assembly
Constitutional Amendment (ACA) 22 Local taxes: limitation, was introduced by
Assembymember Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland and approved by Governor Newsom on June
25, 2026.
Proposition 43 is the result of a compromise between the Governor’s office and the
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which was sponsoring a ballot initiative that would
have made increased the threshold for passage of local tax measures from a simple
majority to a super majority of 66.7% of votes, retroactively. The retroactive nature of the
initiative would have resulted in measures passed with a simple majority since 2017 to be
voided.
As approved on June 25, the proposition will require, starting January 1, 2027, the
approval of a local tax measure with a two-thirds vote. In addition, no local government
or the electorate may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as prescribed by
the California constitution.
This proposition will make it harder for local governments to pass new tax measures. Said
taxes have helped cities to remain fiscally viable and at the same time, maintain high
quality services to their residents.
Over the years, the City of West Hollywood worked to secure voter approval of tax
measures to pay for augmented human services programs aimed at assisting unhoused
individuals. For instance, in 2020, the City included Measure E on the November 3, 2020,
ballot, which enacted a ¾ cent local sales tax to address the COVID-19 shortfall, and
maintain the services West Hollywood residents have indicated are important, such as
addressing homelessness, expanding health and mental health services, retaining local
businesses and jobs, keeping public areas clean and safe, maintaining HIV and AIDS
health services, supporting disaster preparedness, etc. Measure E received 73% of the
total votes cast.
In 2024, and in response to the County’s tax Measure A that repealed Measure H and
Page 7 of 8
increased the County’s sales tax was approved by the voters. At the same time, the City
asked voters to consider supporting Measure WH, Pre-Authorization of a Sales Tax
Measure, which gave preauthorization to the City to redirect 0.25% of the local sales tax
if Measure H sunsets or is repealed. Measure WH passed with overwhelming support of
West Hollywood voters (82%).
Recommendation:
Even though West Hollywood voters have supported the above-mentioned local
measures well above the proposed 66.7% of the votes cast, Proposition 43 would be a
hindrance to many local governments, which rely on limited sources of revenues for the
delivery of services. Therefore, the City Council is recommended to oppose this initiative.
CONFORMANCE WITH VISION 2020 AND THE GOALS OF THE WEST HOLLYWOOD
GENERAL PLAN:
This item is consistent with the Primary Strategic Goal(s) (PSG) and/or Ongoing Strategic
Program(s) (OSP) of:
• OSP-12: Actively Participate in Regional Issues.
In addition, this item is compliant with the following goal(s) of the West Hollywood General
Plan:
• G-1: Ensure that the community is active and engaged in the decision-making process.
EVALUATION PROCESSES:
N/A
ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND HEALTH:
N/A
COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT:
The City’s Communications Department commonly shares City-related information with
the community at large about via its established communication channels, including
Page 8 of 8
posting of information about the City Council’s actions on the City’s web page
www.weho.org
OFFICE OF PRIMARY RESPONSIBILITY:
CITY MANAGER'S DEPARTMENT / CITY MANAGER OFFICE
FISCAL IMPACT:
None.
ATTACHMENT:
None.

Now let me look at some additional critical considerations:

1. The "sham initiative" problem — how much does Prop 43 actually solve it? Well-documented cases: SF Prop G (2018), SD hotel tax (2020), Measure RTM (2026), Oakland Measure E (2026). This is a genuine abuse: local officials route their own tax proposals through "citizen initiative" shells specifically to cut the passage threshold from 66.7% to 50%+1. That's a real integrity problem.

2. The counterargument: majority rule. Special taxes placed on the ballot by government require two-thirds (Prop 13, Prop 218) — voters approved that twice. So Prop 43 essentially just closes an anomaly created by courts. From a "respecting the original will of the voters" perspective, Prop 43 restores what Prop 13/218 voters intended.

But from a "democracy/majority rule" perspective, two-thirds requirements are anti-majoritarian, and California already has too many.

3. The undisclosed ad valorem provision (b) — not mentioned in the LAO analysis or the ballot arguments. This is a transparency concern. What does it do? It bars initiative ad valorem property taxes. Article XIII D §3(a)(1) exception... Let me verify what Art XIII D §3(a)(1) says to know if (b) is essentially a total ban on new voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes (which would foreclose, e.g., a split-roll style commercial property tax or a value-based parcel tax).

Actually — note: Article XIII A, Section 1(a) already caps the ad valorem property tax at 1%, and Article XIII A Section 1(b)(3)? Hmm. And Article XIII A Section 4: "Cities, Counties and special districts may impose a transactions tax or sales tax on the privilege of occupying real property..." wait no.

Let me recall: Article XIII A, Section 4: "Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district, except ad valorem taxes on real property or a transaction tax or sales tax on the sale of real property within such City, County or special district."

So Article XIII A Section 4 already prohibits local governments from imposing ad valorem property taxes and real-property sales taxes. But the Upland line of cases held those restrictions don't apply to voter initiatives. So subdivision (b) of Prop 43's new Section 4.5 extends that prohibition to the electorate exercising the initiative power. So it closes the loophole for property taxes entirely (not just raising the threshold — an outright ban).

Effect: Voters could never again, by initiative, enact a property-value-based tax (e.g., a "mansion tax" structured as ad valorem, or a split-roll reassessment of commercial property). Note Measure ULA is a transaction/transfer tax on sale of real property — which is prohibited by Article XIII A Section 4 too ("a transaction tax or sales tax on the sale of real property"). Interesting: under Prop 43(b), would a voter-initiated transfer tax be barred? The (b) provision only mentions "ad valorem taxes on real property," not transaction/sales taxes. Hmm, so transfer taxes would be allowed but would need two-thirds as special taxes (if earmarked). Actually Measure ULA is earmarked for housing, so it's a special tax; under (a) it would need two-thirds.

Wait — the withdrawn HJTA initiative would have banned charter-city transfer taxes. ACA 22 does not. So transfer taxes remain possible with two-thirds (if special) or majority (if general). Good.

4. Consider: how much does this matter in practice? SPUR notes such measures "account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide." CalMatters says "over two dozen" initiatives passed below two-thirds since 2017. That's a modest number, but they include big ones (LA Measure ULA ~$1.4B raised; SF Prop C).

5. The fiscal effect: LAO says unknown, possibly lower local revenues. The withdrawn initiative would have cost ~$2B/yr; ACA 22 does not.

6. Key political context: The measure was placed on the ballot as part of a deal. Both the author (Wicks) and the Governor (Newsom) who negotiated it now oppose it. Nearly all Democratic groups oppose; business/anti-tax groups support. Yes side raised ~$14M (mostly California Business Roundtable, $9.87M — top donors listed as Peter Thiel and Kim DeGeorge), No side ~$6.7M (SEIU, CTA, building trades, firefighters).

Hmm, interesting: the Yes campaign is heavily funded by the California Business Roundtable — large corporations. That matters: the "taxpayer protection" framing vs. the reality that the biggest funder is a big-business PAC. Note: Prop 43 would also make it harder to tax big business (e.g., SF's gross receipts tax on large businesses for homelessness — Prop C — which passed at 61%). That's a direct corporate interest.

Also note: the No side is heavily funded by public-sector unions, which are also interested in tax revenue to fund their members' wages. Both sides have interested funding.

7. Let's think about who benefits. The citizen-initiative majority threshold has been used both by:
   - Progressive coalitions (housing, homelessness, transit, teacher pay, parks) — Measure ULA, SF Prop C, SF Prop G, Fresno Measure P, Sonoma fire tax
   - But also potentially by businesses or others. In practice, the overwhelming majority of use has been by progressive/local-government-aligned interests to raise revenue for services.
   
   Meanwhile, government officials have used "sham initiatives" to evade the two-thirds requirement — the most troubling abuse (San Diego hotel tax; SF Prop G; Measure RTM).

8. Is there a principled middle? Many analysts note the right fix is holistic reform (as Mercury News says, then still endorses YES). Santa Cruz Sentinel said NO "with reservations," arguing the debate should be holistic.

9. Consider the democratic-principle weighting: A two-thirds requirement is a well-established feature of CA law for government-proposed special taxes. Extending it to initiatives is a coherence argument. But the initiative power is constitutionally reserved (Article II) and has been held to be "liberally construed." Courts have said restrictions on the initiative power must be explicit. Prop 43 would explicitly restrict the initiative power — and would do so permanently (constitutional amendment, can't be repealed by legislature).

10. There's also a "no tax cut" reality: Prop 43 doesn't reduce anyone's taxes. It only makes future increases harder. The Yes argument's claims about "2,000 new taxes in the past decade" and "6% transfer taxes" are misleading: most of those 2,000 were government-placed (already needing two-thirds) or general taxes (unaffected), and Prop 43 doesn't touch charter-city transfer taxes at all (the withdrawn initiative did). So the Yes argument contains claims that don't actually relate to what Prop 43 does. That's a notable accuracy problem — e.g., "Prop 43 protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes" — actually it bars initiative ad valorem property taxes, but transfer taxes are untouched except that special (earmarked) transfer taxes would need two-thirds. And "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" — that's already the law for special taxes; Prop 43 adds no new enforcement. So the Yes argument overstates.

11. On the other hand, the No argument also overstates: "communities would have lost nearly $3 billion a year" (Newsom) — LAO doesn't estimate that; that figure came from the withdrawn retroactive initiative. And claims that it "makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share" is speculative. And the "33.4%" figure: mathematically, blocking a measure requires just over 1/3 of votes cast — accurate in that framing.

Let me verify the "$3 billion" claim and check the LWV recommendation. Also let me check if there's any analysis on whether Prop 43 would affect transit measures like Measure RTM, and check the San Jose council report.

Also — is there anything about Prop 43 possibly being used to reduce taxes? No.

Let me also check whether there's an argument that Prop 43 could hinder tax REPEALS (i.e., voter initiatives to repeal a tax) — that would be an interesting anti-tax angle. The text says "impose, extend, or increase any special tax." A repeal isn't covered. But wait — some have argued that because initiative special taxes would need two-thirds, the practical effect is to entrench existing taxes: e.g., Measure ULA "until ended by voters" — ending it might be a change... Hmm, repealing isn't "imposing, extending, or increasing." Let me check if anyone raised this.

Let me search for a few more things: LWV recommendation, the $3 billion claim, and analysis of whether Prop 43 entrenches existing taxes.

Also let me check the San Jose city council report (they opposed ACA 22?).

And let me look for any legal scholars' views (e.g., Darien Shanske, UC Davis — he wrote "Local Taxes Have Lots of Untapped Potential" and generally supports the majority-vote rule for initiatives).

Let me do these searches.

[{"type":"reasoning.text","text":"Now let me look at some additional critical considerations:

1. The "sham initiative" problem — how much does Prop 43 actually solve it? Well-documented cases: SF Prop G (2018), SD hotel tax (2020), Measure RTM (2026), Oakland Measure E (2026). This is a genuine abuse: local officials route their own tax proposals through "citizen initiative" shells specifically to cut the passage threshold from 66.7% to 50%+1. That's a real integrity problem.

2. The counterargument: majority rule. Special taxes placed on the ballot by government require two-thirds (Prop 13, Prop 218) — voters approved that twice. So Prop 43 essentially just closes an anomaly created by courts. From a "respecting the original will of the voters" perspective, Prop 43 restores what Prop 13/218 voters intended.

But from a "democracy/majority rule" perspective, two-thirds requirements are anti-majoritarian, and California already has too many.

3. The undisclosed ad valorem provision (b) — not mentioned in the LAO analysis or the ballot arguments. This is a transparency concern. What does it do? It bars initiative ad valorem property taxes. Article XIII D §3(a)(1) exception... Let me verify what Art XIII D §3(a)(1) says to know if (b) is essentially a total ban on new voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes (which would foreclose, e.g., a split-roll style commercial property tax or a value-based parcel tax).

Actually — note: Article XIII A, Section 1(a) already caps the ad valorem property tax at 1%, and Article XIII A Section 1(b)(3)? Hmm. And Article XIII A Section 4: "Cities, Counties and special districts may impose a transactions tax or sales tax on the privilege of occupying real property..." wait no.

Let me recall: Article XIII A, Section 4: "Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district, except ad valorem taxes on real property or a transaction tax or sales tax on the sale of real property within such City, County or special district."

So Article XIII A Section 4 already prohibits local governments from imposing ad valorem property taxes and real-property sales taxes. But the Upland line of cases held those restrictions don't apply to voter initiatives. So subdivision (b) of Prop 43's new Section 4.5 extends that prohibition to the electorate exercising the initiative power. So it closes the loophole for property taxes entirely (not just raising the threshold — an outright ban).

Effect: Voters could never again, by initiative, enact a property-value-based tax (e.g., a "mansion tax" structured as ad valorem, or a split-roll reassessment of commercial property). Note Measure ULA is a transaction/transfer tax on sale of real property — which is prohibited by Article XIII A Section 4 too ("a transaction tax or sales tax on the sale of real property"). Interesting: under Prop 43(b), would a voter-initiated transfer tax be barred? The (b) provision only mentions "ad valorem taxes on real property," not transaction/sales taxes. Hmm, so transfer taxes would be allowed but would need two-thirds as special taxes (if earmarked). Actually Measure ULA is earmarked for housing, so it's a special tax; under (a) it would need two-thirds.

Wait — the withdrawn HJTA initiative would have banned charter-city transfer taxes. ACA 22 does not. So transfer taxes remain possible with two-thirds (if special) or majority (if general). Good.

4. Consider: how much does this matter in practice? SPUR notes such measures "account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide." CalMatters says "over two dozen" initiatives passed below two-thirds since 2017. That's a modest number, but they include big ones (LA Measure ULA ~$1.4B raised; SF Prop C).

5. The fiscal effect: LAO says unknown, possibly lower local revenues. The withdrawn initiative would have cost ~$2B/yr; ACA 22 does not.

6. Key political context: The measure was placed on the ballot as part of a deal. Both the author (Wicks) and the Governor (Newsom) who negotiated it now oppose it. Nearly all Democratic groups oppose; business/anti-tax groups support. Yes side raised ~$14M (mostly California Business Roundtable, $9.87M — top donors listed as Peter Thiel and Kim DeGeorge), No side ~$6.7M (SEIU, CTA, building trades, firefighters).

Hmm, interesting: the Yes campaign is heavily funded by the California Business Roundtable — large corporations. That matters: the "taxpayer protection" framing vs. the reality that the biggest funder is a big-business PAC. Note: Prop 43 would also make it harder to tax big business (e.g., SF's gross receipts tax on large businesses for homelessness — Prop C — which passed at 61%). That's a direct corporate interest.

Also note: the No side is heavily funded by public-sector unions, which are also interested in tax revenue to fund their members' wages. Both sides have interested funding.

7. Let's think about who benefits. The citizen-initiative majority threshold has been used both by:
   - Progressive coalitions (housing, homelessness, transit, teacher pay, parks) — Measure ULA, SF Prop C, SF Prop G, Fresno Measure P, Sonoma fire tax
   - But also potentially by businesses or others. In practice, the overwhelming majority of use has been by progressive/local-government-aligned interests to raise revenue for services.
   
   Meanwhile, government officials have used "sham initiatives" to evade the two-thirds requirement — the most troubling abuse (San Diego hotel tax; SF Prop G; Measure RTM).

8. Is there a principled middle? Many analysts note the right fix is holistic reform (as Mercury News says, then still endorses YES). Santa Cruz Sentinel said NO "with reservations," arguing the debate should be holistic.

9. Consider the democratic-principle weighting: A two-thirds requirement is a well-established feature of CA law for government-proposed special taxes. Extending it to initiatives is a coherence argument. But the initiative power is constitutionally reserved (Article II) and has been held to be "liberally construed." Courts have said restrictions on the initiative power must be explicit. Prop 43 would explicitly restrict the initiative power — and would do so permanently (constitutional amendment, can't be repealed by legislature).

10. There's also a "no tax cut" reality: Prop 43 doesn't reduce anyone's taxes. It only makes future increases harder. The Yes argument's claims about "2,000 new taxes in the past decade" and "6% transfer taxes" are misleading: most of those 2,000 were government-placed (already needing two-thirds) or general taxes (unaffected), and Prop 43 doesn't touch charter-city transfer taxes at all (the withdrawn initiative did). So the Yes argument contains claims that don't actually relate to what Prop 43 does. That's a notable accuracy problem — e.g., "Prop 43 protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes" — actually it bars initiative ad valorem property taxes, but transfer taxes are untouched except that special (earmarked) transfer taxes would need two-thirds. And "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" — that's already the law for special taxes; Prop 43 adds no new enforcement. So the Yes argument overstates.

11. On the other hand, the No argument also overstates: "communities would have lost nearly $3 billion a year" (Newsom) — LAO doesn't estimate that; that figure came from the withdrawn retroactive initiative. And claims that it "makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share" is speculative. And the "33.4%" figure: mathematically, blocking a measure requires just over 1/3 of votes cast — accurate in that framing.

Let me verify the "$3 billion" claim and check the LWV recommendation. Also let me check if there's any analysis on whether Prop 43 would affect transit measures like Measure RTM, and check the San Jose council report.

Also — is there anything about Prop 43 possibly being used to reduce taxes? No.

Let me also check whether there's an argument that Prop 43 could hinder tax REPEALS (i.e., voter initiatives to repeal a tax) — that would be an interesting anti-tax angle. The text says "impose, extend, or increase any special tax." A repeal isn't covered. But wait — some have argued that because initiative special taxes would need two-thirds, the practical effect is to entrench existing taxes: e.g., Measure ULA "until ended by voters" — ending it might be a change... Hmm, repealing isn't "imposing, extending, or increasing." Let me check if anyone raised this.

Let me search for a few more things: LWV recommendation, the $3 billion claim, and analysis of whether Prop 43 entrenches existing taxes.

Also let me check the San Jose city council report (they opposed ACA 22?).

And let me look for any legal scholars' views (e.g., Darien Shanske, UC Davis — he wrote "Local Taxes Have Lots of Untapped Potential" and generally supports the majority-vote rule for initiatives).

Let me do these searches.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

Now let me look at some additional critical considerations:

1. The "sham initiative" problem — how much does Prop 43 actually solve it? Well-documented cases: SF Prop G (2018), SD hotel tax (2020), Measure RTM (2026), Oakland Measure E (2026). This is a genuine abuse: local officials route their own tax proposals through "citizen initiative" shells specifically to cut the passage threshold from 66.7% to 50%+1. That's a real integrity problem.

2. The counterargument: majority rule. Special taxes placed on the ballot by government require two-thirds (Prop 13, Prop 218) — voters approved that twice. So Prop 43 essentially just closes an anomaly created by courts. From a "respecting the original will of the voters" perspective, Prop 43 restores what Prop 13/218 voters intended.

But from a "democracy/majority rule" perspective, two-thirds requirements are anti-majoritarian, and California already has too many.

3. The undisclosed ad valorem provision (b) — not mentioned in the LAO analysis or the ballot arguments. This is a transparency concern. What does it do? It bars initiative ad valorem property taxes. Article XIII D §3(a)(1) exception... Let me verify what Art XIII D §3(a)(1) says to know if (b) is essentially a total ban on new voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes (which would foreclose, e.g., a split-roll style commercial property tax or a value-based parcel tax).

Actually — note: Article XIII A, Section 1(a) already caps the ad valorem property tax at 1%, and Article XIII A Section 1(b)(3)? Hmm. And Article XIII A Section 4: "Cities, Counties and special districts may impose a transactions tax or sales tax on the privilege of occupying real property..." wait no.

Let me recall: Article XIII A, Section 4: "Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district, except ad valorem taxes on real property or a transaction tax or sales tax on the sale of real property within such City, County or special district."

So Article XIII A Section 4 already prohibits local governments from imposing ad valorem property taxes and real-property sales taxes. But the Upland line of cases held those restrictions don't apply to voter initiatives. So subdivision (b) of Prop 43's new Section 4.5 extends that prohibition to the electorate exercising the initiative power. So it closes the loophole for property taxes entirely (not just raising the threshold — an outright ban).

Effect: Voters could never again, by initiative, enact a property-value-based tax (e.g., a "mansion tax" structured as ad valorem, or a split-roll reassessment of commercial property). Note Measure ULA is a transaction/transfer tax on sale of real property — which is prohibited by Article XIII A Section 4 too ("a transaction tax or sales tax on the sale of real property"). Interesting: under Prop 43(b), would a voter-initiated transfer tax be barred? The (b) provision only mentions "ad valorem taxes on real property," not transaction/sales taxes. Hmm, so transfer taxes would be allowed but would need two-thirds as special taxes (if earmarked). Actually Measure ULA is earmarked for housing, so it's a special tax; under (a) it would need two-thirds.

Wait — the withdrawn HJTA initiative would have banned charter-city transfer taxes. ACA 22 does not. So transfer taxes remain possible with two-thirds (if special) or majority (if general). Good.

4. Consider: how much does this matter in practice? SPUR notes such measures "account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide." CalMatters says "over two dozen" initiatives passed below two-thirds since 2017. That's a modest number, but they include big ones (LA Measure ULA ~$1.4B raised; SF Prop C).

5. The fiscal effect: LAO says unknown, possibly lower local revenues. The withdrawn initiative would have cost ~$2B/yr; ACA 22 does not.

6. Key political context: The measure was placed on the ballot as part of a deal. Both the author (Wicks) and the Governor (Newsom) who negotiated it now oppose it. Nearly all Democratic groups oppose; business/anti-tax groups support. Yes side raised ~$14M (mostly California Business Roundtable, $9.87M — top donors listed as Peter Thiel and Kim DeGeorge), No side ~$6.7M (SEIU, CTA, building trades, firefighters).

Hmm, interesting: the Yes campaign is heavily funded by the California Business Roundtable — large corporations. That matters: the "taxpayer protection" framing vs. the reality that the biggest funder is a big-business PAC. Note: Prop 43 would also make it harder to tax big business (e.g., SF's gross receipts tax on large businesses for homelessness — Prop C — which passed at 61%). That's a direct corporate interest.

Also note: the No side is heavily funded by public-sector unions, which are also interested in tax revenue to fund their members' wages. Both sides have interested funding.

7. Let's think about who benefits. The citizen-initiative majority threshold has been used both by:
   - Progressive coalitions (housing, homelessness, transit, teacher pay, parks) — Measure ULA, SF Prop C, SF Prop G, Fresno Measure P, Sonoma fire tax
   - But also potentially by businesses or others. In practice, the overwhelming majority of use has been by progressive/local-government-aligned interests to raise revenue for services.
   
   Meanwhile, government officials have used "sham initiatives" to evade the two-thirds requirement — the most troubling abuse (San Diego hotel tax; SF Prop G; Measure RTM).

8. Is there a principled middle? Many analysts note the right fix is holistic reform (as Mercury News says, then still endorses YES). Santa Cruz Sentinel said NO "with reservations," arguing the debate should be holistic.

9. Consider the democratic-principle weighting: A two-thirds requirement is a well-established feature of CA law for government-proposed special taxes. Extending it to initiatives is a coherence argument. But the initiative power is constitutionally reserved (Article II) and has been held to be "liberally construed." Courts have said restrictions on the initiative power must be explicit. Prop 43 would explicitly restrict the initiative power — and would do so permanently (constitutional amendment, can't be repealed by legislature).

10. There's also a "no tax cut" reality: Prop 43 doesn't reduce anyone's taxes. It only makes future increases harder. The Yes argument's claims about "2,000 new taxes in the past decade" and "6% transfer taxes" are misleading: most of those 2,000 were government-placed (already needing two-thirds) or general taxes (unaffected), and Prop 43 doesn't touch charter-city transfer taxes at all (the withdrawn initiative did). So the Yes argument contains claims that don't actually relate to what Prop 43 does. That's a notable accuracy problem — e.g., "Prop 43 protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes" — actually it bars initiative ad valorem property taxes, but transfer taxes are untouched except that special (earmarked) transfer taxes would need two-thirds. And "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" — that's already the law for special taxes; Prop 43 adds no new enforcement. So the Yes argument overstates.

11. On the other hand, the No argument also overstates: "communities would have lost nearly $3 billion a year" (Newsom) — LAO doesn't estimate that; that figure came from the withdrawn retroactive initiative. And claims that it "makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share" is speculative. And the "33.4%" figure: mathematically, blocking a measure requires just over 1/3 of votes cast — accurate in that framing.

Let me verify the "$3 billion" claim and check the LWV recommendation. Also let me check if there's any analysis on whether Prop 43 would affect transit measures like Measure RTM, and check the San Jose council report.

Also — is there anything about Prop 43 possibly being used to reduce taxes? No.

Let me also check whether there's an argument that Prop 43 could hinder tax REPEALS (i.e., voter initiatives to repeal a tax) — that would be an interesting anti-tax angle. The text says "impose, extend, or increase any special tax." A repeal isn't covered. But wait — some have argued that because initiative special taxes would need two-thirds, the practical effect is to entrench existing taxes: e.g., Measure ULA "until ended by voters" — ending it might be a change... Hmm, repealing isn't "imposing, extending, or increasing." Let me check if anyone raised this.

Let me search for a few more things: LWV recommendation, the $3 billion claim, and analysis of whether Prop 43 entrenches existing taxes.

Also let me check the San Jose city council report (they opposed ACA 22?).

And let me look for any legal scholars' views (e.g., Darien Shanske, UC Davis — he wrote "Local Taxes Have Lots of Untapped Potential" and generally supports the majority-vote rule for initiatives).

Home (https://calbudgetcenter.org/) / Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/) / Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.
table of contents
What Would Proposition 43 Do?
Glossary of Key Terms
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Proposition 43 Do?
This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Under California’s Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C), all taxes levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop. 43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to any taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.
Glossary of Key Terms
General tax
Local voter initiative process
Parcel tax
Simple majority vote
Special tax
Supermajority vote
General tax
A tax that is levied by a city or county and that may be spent on any program or service. All non-property taxes that cities and counties may levy can be imposed as general taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) . A general tax may be approved by a simple majority of local voters, regardless of whether it is placed on the ballot by the local government entity or by a local voter initiative.
Local voter initiative process
Gives residents of a city or a county the power to propose changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2011.&article=II) to local ordinances. This process involves a number of steps, including drafting a ballot measure, circulating petitions, and gathering the required signatures.
Parcel tax
A tax on a parcel of property that is not based on the property value. This tax is generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square-foot or per-room basis. Parcel taxes can be levied by cities, counties, school districts, community college districts, and most special districts. Parcel taxes are always considered to be special taxes for the purpose of determining voter-approval requirements.
Simple majority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive support from at least half of voters plus one additional voter (50%+1) in order to be approved.
Special tax
Includes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) 1) parcel taxes, 2) city or county taxes (excluding property taxes) dedicated to specific purposes, and 3) taxes (excluding property taxes) levied by special purpose districts — that is, special districts, K-12 school districts, and community college districts.
Supermajority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive more than a simple majority vote, such as three-fifths or two-thirds, in order to be approved.
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
California’s Constitution has a complex set of rules governing how local governments can raise taxes and other types of revenue. These rules were put in place by statewide ballot measures over the past several decades (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Major%20Milestones%20in%20the%20Development%20of%20Voter%E2%80%93Approval%20Requirements%20for%20Local%20Taxes), beginning with Prop. 13 in 1978 and followed by other measures creating additional restrictions on local revenue-raising capacity, including Prop. 62 (1986) and Prop. 218 (1996).
These rules apply to local measures to create new taxes as well as to increase or extend any existing tax.
Tax measures proposed by local governments — such as city councils or county boards of supervisors — must go on the ballot and be approved by voters. Current voter-approval thresholds differ depending on the type of tax that would be raised:
A general tax requires only a simple majority vote to pass, with the revenue available for any program or service.
A special tax requires a two-thirds vote to pass, and includes a tax dedicated to a specific purpose.
Special taxes proposed through the local voter initiative process are subject to different rules. In recent years, a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) have clarified that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in the state Constitution does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative. Therefore, both general taxes and special taxes proposed by voters can be approved with a simple majority vote . 2 (javascript:void(0)) Several cases involving special tax voter initiatives that were approved with a simple majority vote were appealed to the California Supreme Court, but the Supreme Court denied review of the appellate court decisions, allowing these decisions to stand. A variety of special tax initiatives have been approved over the past several years with a simple majority vote, such as:
San Francisco’s Measure C in November 2018, creating a tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, which passed with 51% of the vote.
Fresno’s Measure P in November 2018, increasing the local sales tax rate to fund community parks, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Los Angeles’ Measure ULA in November 2022, creating a property transfer tax on sales of high-value property to raise funds for affordable housing development and homelessness service, which passed with 58% of the vote.
Madera County’s Measure T in November 2024, renewing a local sales tax rate to fund transportation projects, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Certain types of local taxes are always classified as special taxes for the purposes of voter approval requirements. This includes:
Taxes levied by special-purpose districts, including school districts, community college districts, and special districts.
Parcel taxes, which are taxes on parcels of property that are not based on the property value . These taxes are generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square foot or per-room basis.
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
Californians in every community across the state benefit from services provided by local governments. Local services help keep people safe and healthy by providing fire protection, law enforcement, public health services, hospitals and emergency services, road safety, and more. Local governments also provide educational and recreational spaces like public libraries, public parks, and playgrounds.
Californians experiencing economic insecurity, food security, or who don’t have access to private health insurance can access financial assistance, food assistance, and health care because counties are there to administer public health and economic security programs. Cities can support the development of affordable housing to ensure more of their residents can afford a safe place to live.
The services provided by California’s local governments vary according to the type of entity (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/who_does_what.pdf):
Counties administer health and human services programs such as Medi-Cal (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/medi-cal/) health coverage, CalFresh (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calfresh/) food assistance, and CalWORKs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calworks/) cash assistance for families. Counties also provide public health, behavioral health, and child welfare services. Additionally, counties are responsible (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-county-budget-process-guide/) for overseeing the local justice system and courts, administering elections, and providing municipal services like sewer systems and trash pick-up in unincorporated areas.
Cities provide a variety of municipal services such as fire protection, housing and urban planning, parks and recreation, libraries, street repair, water and sewer systems, and law enforcement — although some of these services may be provided by special districts in some areas.
Special districts provide specialized services such as fire protection, water, electricity, parks and recreation, transit, hospitals, and other health care services.
Regional entities such as Joint Powers Authorities and Councils of Government coordinate policy and service provision across regions spanning multiple cities or counties, such as regional transportation authorities.
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
Local governments in California rely on a variety of revenue sources, including transfers from the state and federal governments, allocations of local property taxes, and various other taxes, service charges, assessments, and fees.
Most types of local governments receive some revenues from the local property tax, capped at 1% by Prop. 13 (1978). Property taxes are collected by counties and the revenues are allocated (https://propertytax.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2026/revenue/0/entity_type?vis=pieChart) to support city and county governments, school districts, community college districts, and special districts in accordance with formulas established in state law. Local governments and voters cannot increase property taxes beyond the 1% rate, except to finance infrastructure bonds. 3 (javascript:void(0)) Property tax increases to support school infrastructure bonds can generally be approved by 55% of local voters. All other property taxes for infrastructure bonds must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
Curious About Other Ballot Propositions?
Browse our collection of resources covering California’s statewide ballot measures to help you understand what’s at stake for California this November.
See More Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/)
Other common types of taxes supporting local services include sales taxes (known as transactions and use taxes at the local level), taxes on hotel stays (known as transient occupancy taxes), property transfer taxes, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
The revenues that make up local government budgets vary by the type of entity (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Local%20Governments%20Levy%20Many%20Types%20of%20Taxes), and the legal authority to raise taxes (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/resources__Revenues_and_Responsibilities.pdf) also differs by government type. Cities and counties have fairly broad authority to raise a variety of taxes — with voter approval — while special districts have more limited authority. These districts are largely limited to parcel taxes — a tax on parcels of land not based on their value — as a source of discretionary revenue, although some can levy district sales taxes and certain other types of taxes.
More than half of county-level revenues (https://counties.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/category?vis=pieChart) statewide come from the state and federal governments and local property taxes. Other types of taxes make up a small share of total county revenues — generally less than 3%. Common types of taxes levied by counties include sales taxes, property transfer taxes, taxes on hotel stays, and utility user taxes.
City-level revenues (https://cities.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_1?vis=pieChart) primarily come from service charges for municipal functions — such as electricity, water, and sewer services — and various taxes. These two categories generally each make up around one-third of total city revenues statewide. Local property tax revenues and sales taxes are the largest sources of tax revenues for cities, each representing about one-quarter of tax revenues. Other major tax revenue sources for cities include taxes on hotel stays, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
Special district revenues (https://districts.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_2?vis=pieChart) come largely from customer service charges for the service provided by the district, local property taxes, and certain other taxes and assessments, depending on the type of district. 4 (javascript:void(0)) The composition of special district revenues depends on the type of special district (https://sgf.senate.ca.gov/sites/sgf.senate.ca.gov/files/special_district_facts_2016.pdf). Enterprise districts provide services to customers for a charge and operate similar to businesses, being largely financed by user charges. Examples of enterprise districts include health care districts, airport districts, water districts, and other utility districts. Non-enterprise districts provide benefits to entire communities — such as fire protection and road repair services — and are primarily funded by property taxes and other types of taxes and assessments. As noted above, taxes levied by special districts are always considered special taxes so they require approval of two-thirds of voters in the district, unless they are placed on the ballot by voters.
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Would Make It More Difficult for Communities to Generate Revenues to Meet Local Needs
California already imposes high barriers to raising local revenues by requiring all special taxes levied by local governments to be approved by two-thirds of voters instead of a simple majority, and by classifying certain types of taxes — parcel taxes and taxes levied by special districts and school districts — as special taxes subject to higher vote requirements. Extending the two-thirds vote requirement to voter-initiated special tax proposals, as Prop. 43 proposes, would decrease the likelihood that these measures would pass, even if a significant majority of local voters support the measure and the services that the new revenues would fund.
In contrast to the high bar for raising taxes, local governments do not need voter approval to reduce services — and cuts to services often result when localities face revenue shortfalls. Yet, communities also have the option of raising revenues to help close budget gaps. If Prop. 43 passes, counties and cities would still have the ability to raise general taxes with approval from a simple majority of voters to shore up local services. However, local voters’ ability to propose new special taxes to protect or strengthen key services would be limited as local voter initiatives would become much more challenging to pass. Additionally, voters in special districts would face a higher bar to increase revenues to preserve and expand services, regardless of whether the funds would be targeted to specific programs.
Proposition 43’s Constraints on Local Revenues Would Make Things Harder for Communities Already Struggling
Governments across the board have felt the impacts of inflation on the costs of providing public services, and the state’s aging population increasing the cost of providing some services such as health care. The impacts of the 2025 federal budget reconciliation law, (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/hr1-and-the-federal-budget-how-california-leaders-can-respond-to-trumps-cuts/) H.R. 1 — also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — along with the effects of climate change, the labor market (https://immresearch.org/reports/ice-arrests-result-in-a-decline-in-employment-state-level-projections/) and broader economic impacts (https://www.bayareaeconomy.org/files/pdf/Economic%20Impact%20of%20Mass%20Deportation_June%202025.pdf) of arrests and deportations of immigrants, and other federal policy changes such as tariffs, are also creating challenges for localities.
H.R. 1 will deeply harm Californians by cutting funding for essential health care and food assistance programs, primarily Medi-Cal and CalFresh, pushing more people into poverty and widenin

THE SITUATION
California faces a housing shortage, and home

incomes. For many people, saving enough

operates programs that help some Californians
purchase homes. Some of these programs
provide down-payment assistance through loans

programs focus on low- and moderate-income
households.
California law also establishes construction

a new homeownership assistance program.

participants rather than taxpayers.

• Eligible buyers could receive a second
mortgage worth up to 17% of the
purchase price of a qualifying newly built

• Buyers would have to make a minimum
3% down payment from their own funds.
• Borrowers would have to meet income

residence, and be California residents.

Prop 37 would likely have no direct state or local
government cost. The measure is designed so
that homeowners who receive loans would repay
the bonds and administrative costs through their
mortgage payments.
The ultimate impact of the program will depend
on factors such as investor demand for the
bonds, participation by homebuyers, and
whether the measure increases home
construction and homeownership.

Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.

What Would Proposition 43 Do?
This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Under California’s Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C), all taxes levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop. 43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to any taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.
Glossary of Key Terms
General tax
Local voter initiative process
Parcel tax
Simple majority vote
Special tax
Supermajority vote
General tax
A tax that is levied by a city or county and that may be spent on any program or service. All non-property taxes that cities and counties may levy can be imposed as general taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) . A general tax may be approved by a simple majority of local voters, regardless of whether it is placed on the ballot by the local government entity or by a local voter initiative.
Local voter initiative process
Gives residents of a city or a county the power to propose changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2011.&article=II) to local ordinances. This process involves a number of steps, including drafting a ballot measure, circulating petitions, and gathering the required signatures.
Parcel tax
A tax on a parcel of property that is not based on the property value. This tax is generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square-foot or per-room basis. Parcel taxes can be levied by cities, counties, school districts, community college districts, and most special districts. Parcel taxes are always considered to be special taxes for the purpose of determining voter-approval requirements.
Simple majority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive support from at least half of voters plus one additional voter (50%+1) in order to be approved.
Special tax
Includes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) 1) parcel taxes, 2) city or county taxes (excluding property taxes) dedicated to specific purposes, and 3) taxes (excluding property taxes) levied by special purpose districts — that is, special districts, K-12 school districts, and community college districts.
Supermajority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive more than a simple majority vote, such as three-fifths or two-thirds, in order to be approved.
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
California’s Constitution has a complex set of rules governing how local governments can raise taxes and other types of revenue. These rules were put in place by statewide ballot measures over the past several decades (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Major%20Milestones%20in%20the%20Development%20of%20Voter%E2%80%93Approval%20Requirements%20for%20Local%20Taxes), beginning with Prop. 13 in 1978 and followed by other measures creating additional restrictions on local revenue-raising capacity, including Prop. 62 (1986) and Prop. 218 (1996).
These rules apply to local measures to create new taxes as well as to increase or extend any existing tax.
Tax measures proposed by local governments — such as city councils or county boards of supervisors — must go on the ballot and be approved by voters. Current voter-approval thresholds differ depending on the type of tax that would be raised:
A general tax requires only a simple majority vote to pass, with the revenue available for any program or service.
A special tax requires a two-thirds vote to pass, and includes a tax dedicated to a specific purpose.
Special taxes proposed through the local voter initiative process are subject to different rules. In recent years, a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) have clarified that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in the state Constitution does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative. Therefore, both general taxes and special taxes proposed by voters can be approved with a simple majority vote . 2 (javascript:void(0)) Several cases involving special tax voter initiatives that were approved with a simple majority vote were appealed to the California Supreme Court, but the Supreme Court denied review of the appellate court decisions, allowing these decisions to stand. A variety of special tax initiatives have been approved over the past several years with a simple majority vote, such as:
San Francisco’s Measure C in November 2018, creating a tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, which passed with 51% of the vote.
Fresno’s Measure P in November 2018, increasing the local sales tax rate to fund community parks, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Los Angeles’ Measure ULA in November 2022, creating a property transfer tax on sales of high-value property to raise funds for affordable housing development and homelessness service, which passed with 58% of the vote.
Madera County’s Measure T in November 2024, renewing a local sales tax rate to fund transportation projects, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Certain types of local taxes are always classified as special taxes for the purposes of voter approval requirements. This includes:
Taxes levied by special-purpose districts, including school districts, community college districts, and special districts.
Parcel taxes, which are taxes on parcels of property that are not based on the property value . These taxes are generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square foot or per-room basis.
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
Californians in every community across the state benefit from services provided by local governments. Local services help keep people safe and healthy by providing fire protection, law enforcement, public health services, hospitals and emergency services, road safety, and more. Local governments also provide educational and recreational spaces like public libraries, public parks, and playgrounds.
Californians experiencing economic insecurity, food security, or who don’t have access to private health insurance can access financial assistance, food assistance, and health care because counties are there to administer public health and economic security programs. Cities can support the development of affordable housing to ensure more of their residents can afford a safe place to live.
The services provided by California’s local governments vary according to the type of entity (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/who_does_what.pdf):
Counties administer health and human services programs such as Medi-Cal (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/medi-cal/) health coverage, CalFresh (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calfresh/) food assistance, and CalWORKs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calworks/) cash assistance for families. Counties also provide public health, behavioral health, and child welfare services. Additionally, counties are responsible (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-county-budget-process-guide/) for overseeing the local justice system and courts, administering elections, and providing municipal services like sewer systems and trash pick-up in unincorporated areas.
Cities provide a variety of municipal services such as fire protection, housing and urban planning, parks and recreation, libraries, street repair, water and sewer systems, and law enforcement — although some of these services may be provided by special districts in some areas.
Special districts provide specialized services such as fire protection, water, electricity, parks and recreation, transit, hospitals, and other health care services.
Regional entities such as Joint Powers Authorities and Councils of Government coordinate policy and service provision across regions spanning multiple cities or counties, such as regional transportation authorities.
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
Local governments in California rely on a variety of revenue sources, including transfers from the state and federal governments, allocations of local property taxes, and various other taxes, service charges, assessments, and fees.
Most types of local governments receive some revenues from the local property tax, capped at 1% by Prop. 13 (1978). Property taxes are collected by counties and the revenues are allocated (https://propertytax.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2026/revenue/0/entity_type?vis=pieChart) to support city and county governments, school districts, community college districts, and special districts in accordance with formulas established in state law. Local governments and voters cannot increase property taxes beyond the 1% rate, except to finance infrastructure bonds. 3 (javascript:void(0)) Property tax increases to support school infrastructure bonds can generally be approved by 55% of local voters. All other property taxes for infrastructure bonds must be approved by two-thirds of voters.

Other common types of taxes supporting local services include sales taxes (known as transactions and use taxes at the local level), taxes on hotel stays (known as transient occupancy taxes), property transfer taxes, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
The revenues that make up local government budgets vary by the type of entity (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Local%20Governments%20Levy%20Many%20Types%20of%20Taxes), and the legal authority to raise taxes (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/resources__Revenues_and_Responsibilities.pdf) also differs by government type. Cities and counties have fairly broad authority to raise a variety of taxes — with voter approval — while special districts have more limited authority. These districts are largely limited to parcel taxes — a tax on parcels of land not based on their value — as a source of discretionary revenue, although some can levy district sales taxes and certain other types of taxes.
More than half of county-level revenues (https://counties.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/category?vis=pieChart) statewide come from the state and federal governments and local property taxes. Other types of taxes make up a small share of total county revenues — generally less than 3%. Common types of taxes levied by counties include sales taxes, property transfer taxes, taxes on hotel stays, and utility user taxes.
City-level revenues (https://cities.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_1?vis=pieChart) primarily come from service charges for municipal functions — such as electricity, water, and sewer services — and various taxes. These two categories generally each make up around one-third of total city revenues statewide. Local property tax revenues and sales taxes are the largest sources of tax revenues for cities, each representing about one-quarter of tax revenues. Other major tax revenue sources for cities include taxes on hotel stays, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
Special district revenues (https://districts.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_2?vis=pieChart) come largely from customer service charges for the service provided by the district, local property taxes, and certain other taxes and assessments, depending on the type of district. 4 (javascript:void(0)) The composition of special district revenues depends on the type of special district (https://sgf.senate.ca.gov/sites/sgf.senate.ca.gov/files/special_district_facts_2016.pdf). Enterprise districts provide services to customers for a charge and operate similar to businesses, being largely financed by user charges. Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.
