Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. The opposing view: A city councilmember from Sonoma believes Prop. 43 enables minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/), making it harder to fund vital government functions . Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. # 2026 California Proposition 43
**Proposition 43** is a proposed legislative constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.
Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under Proposition 13 for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local initiative power.^[1]^ Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the California Constitution.^[2]^
Proposition 43 was proposed to overturn appellate court rulings following the 2017 *Upland* decision by the California Supreme Court,^[3]^ which created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13.
These appellate court rulings held that citizen-led special tax proposals under the local initiative power were no longer subject to the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13.

Learn more here (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/). California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. The opposing view: A city councilmember from Sonoma believes Prop. 43 enables minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/), making it harder to fund vital government functions . Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Very helpful. Now I know:
- The ad valorem provision: "citizens cannot use a ballot initiative to establish a new property tax based on the value of real property." So it's a ban on voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes. Note: local governments already can't (Article XIII A §4). So this closes the initiative loophole for property taxes entirely.
- Real-world example: Santa Clara Valley Open Space Authority Measure D — a parcel tax of $0.02/sq ft for open space, wildfire and flood prevention, trails — passed by 55% on June 2, 2026 via citizen initiative. Under Prop 43 it would have failed.
- Connect Bay Area regional transit measure (Measure RTM) — a citizen-initiated transit sales tax on Nov 2026 ballot, unaffected by Prop 43 (already qualified).

Now let me think about the decision framework.

Key considerations:

FOR (YES):
1. Consistency: A special tax is a special tax; the route to the ballot shouldn't determine the threshold. Voters approved two-thirds for local special taxes in Prop 13 (1978), Prop 62 (1986), Prop 218 (1996). Courts (Upland line) created a distinction nobody voted for.
2. Closes a documented abuse: government officials and unions/developers route their own tax proposals through "sham citizen initiatives" specifically to halve the passage threshold. Examples: SF supervisors' Prop G (2018 commercial rent tax for childcare, passed 51%); San Diego's hotel tax (2020, 65.2% declared failed then upheld); Measure RTM (2026 transit tax funded by transit unions/contractors rather than MTC); Oakland Measure E (2026).
3. Legitimacy/consensus: earmarked taxes lock money into a specific purpose, reducing budget flexibility for decades. A higher consensus bar is arguably appropriate for that.
4. Narrow and prospective: doesn't repeal any existing tax; doesn't touch general taxes; doesn't touch transfer taxes as the withdrawn initiative would have.
5. Big-business funding on the Yes side suggests it's about protecting corporate taxpayers from gross-receipts/business taxes passed by majority (e.g., SF Prop C at 61%). That is a genuine taxpayer-protection effect.

AGAINST (NO):
1. Anti-majoritarian: entrenches a supermajority requirement, letting ~34% of voters block what 66% support. It permanently writes into the constitution a restriction on the initiative power — one of the few checks on legislatures. Constitutional amendment: the Legislature can't fix it later; only voters can.
2. It's a permanent, one-way ratchet toward Prop 13's already-dysfunctional structure — at exactly the moment California faces ~$30B/yr in federal Medi-Cal cuts from H.R. 1 and local governments face rising costs (wildfire, homelessness, infrastructure). The state and locals have extremely constrained revenue tools; Prop 43 removes one of the few remaining ones.
3. Perverse incentives: After Prop 43, dedicated/earmarked (more accountable, more transparent) taxes need two-thirds, while unrestricted general taxes need only a majority. So Prop 43 pushes communities toward less-accountable general taxes. Both SPUR and even the Mercury News (which endorsed YES) acknowledge this is "backwards."
4. Undisclosed second provision: subdivision (b) bans all voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes. The LAO's analysis, the official title/summary, and neither ballot argument mention it. That's a meaningful hidden change — it permanently forecloses, e.g., a future voter initiative to tax commercial property at value (split-roll style) or any value-based property tax. Voting YES on a constitutional amendment whose operative provisions are not described in the ballot materials is a transparency problem.
5. Real-world casualties: documented measures that would have failed — LA Measure ULA (58%, raised $1.4B for affordable housing/homelessness), SF Prop C (61%, homelessness services), SF Prop G (60.76%, teacher pay), Fresno Measure P (52%, parks), Sonoma County fire/wildfire sales tax (62%, 2024), Alameda County hospital parcel tax (64.7%, 2025), Santa Clara Valley Open Space Authority Measure D (55%, wildfire/flood/open space, 2026), Madera County transportation sales tax (52%, 2024). Many of these are exactly the services Californians say they want: wildfire response, hospitals, teachers, housing.
6. Who's behind it and who benefits: Yes campaign ~$14M, with ~$9.9M from the California Business Roundtable Issues PAC (top donors Peter Thiel, Kim DeGeorge) plus $1M each from Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett (large real estate owners). The measure originated as a real-estate industry campaign against LA's mansion tax. The "taxpayer protection" framing is largely funded by the corporate taxpayers who'd be protected. Meanwhile, the measure's own author (Buffy Wicks) and the Governor who brokered the deal (Newsom) now oppose it. The Legislature passed it 68–2 / 35–1 not as an endorsement of policy but as a hostage trade to kill a far worse retroactive initiative — and the Yes campaign's argument touts that near-unanimous vote as evidence of merit, which is misleading.
7. The Yes argument contains claims not supported by the measure: "over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade" (most weren't citizen-initiated special taxes, the only kind affected); "protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes" / "some cities charge transfer taxes as high as 6%" (Prop 43 does NOT cap transfer taxes — the withdrawn initiative did); "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" (already true for special taxes; Prop 43 adds no enforcement). So the official argument materially overstates what the measure does.
8. It doesn't lower anyone's taxes. It's purely a future procedural constraint.
9. Even the pro-43 Mercury News editorial frames the correct solution as holistic reform of Prop 13 decided by voters — yet Prop 43 moves in the opposite direction, making the structure more rigid. The Santa Cruz Sentinel board was divided and recommended NO, saying the debate "should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal."
10. Editorial/organizational balance: NO — Sacramento Bee/McClatchy boards, LA Times (Skelton: no), LWV California, ACLU SoCal, SPUR, CA Democratic Party, firefighters, teachers, nurses, Cal Cities/League of California Cities, CSDA, cities of Berkeley and West Hollywood, Press Democrat, Santa Barbara Independent, George Skelton. YES — Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, Daily Bulletin/Southern California News Group, Howard Jarvis, Reform California, CA Republican Party, CalTax, CA Small Business Association, CA Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, Family Business Assn.
11. Polling: PPIC Oct: 42% yes / 55% no; IGS/LAT Oct: 36% yes / 46% no. Voters trend against it as they learn about it.

Counter-consideration for YES: Is the "sham initiative" problem serious enough to justify permanently restricting the initiative power? I think the answer is that the problem is real but is better solved by targeted anti-evasion legislation (e.g., rules barring government-official-sponsored initiatives, as courts already scrutinize) rather than a constitutional supermajority requirement that applies to all genuine grassroots initiatives too. Also note: California already has two-thirds for government-proposed special taxes, and Prop 43 wouldn't change that. The initiative path is the only escape valve, and it's the one designed for exactly the case where elected officials won't act.

Also, note the asymmetry: The two-thirds rule for government-proposed special taxes came from Prop 13/62/218 — voter-approved. Extending it to initiatives is arguably "restoring voter intent." But the courts held that the initiative power is reserved and restrictions must be explicit; and voters have repeatedly rejected expanding Prop 13-style limits (e.g., they killed split-roll... no wait, they killed Prop 15 in 2020 which would have loosened Prop 13; and they killed the 2024 Taxpayer Protection Act via court). Hmm — actually the courts removed the 2024 measure, so voters never got to vote. And voters approved Prop 13, 62, 218 — so on balance, California voters have historically supported tax-limiting measures. But those all applied to government-proposed taxes.

One more consideration: the "majority rule" principle vs. "supermajority for taxes." Many democracies require supermajorities for tax increases at the legislative level. But here it's the voters themselves voting. Restricting what a majority of voters can decide is a serious limitation on popular sovereignty, permanently entrenched in the constitution.

Another consideration: does Prop 43 apply to school district parcel taxes? Parcel taxes for school districts: currently, school district parcel taxes require 55% under Proposition 39? No — Prop 39 (2000) is for GO bonds at 55%. School parcel taxes require two-thirds under Art XIII C (they're special taxes) when placed by the district; when placed by initiative, majority. Hmm, actually school parcel taxes are almost always placed by the district, requiring two-thirds. So Prop 43 mostly affects citizen initiatives.

Important: For special districts, ALL taxes are special taxes (per Art XIII C §1(d)). So Prop 43 means any voter-initiated tax for a special district needs two-thirds. That includes fire districts, transit districts, hospital districts, open space districts. That's a significant constraint.

Also note the LAO's analysis omitted subdivision (b) entirely. That's a notable gap.

Let me do one more check: I want to verify the claim about the Yes campaign's top funder and Newsom's statement, and check whether there are any additional recent developments (e.g., legal challenges to Prop 43, or a court ruling). Also let me check the ACLU SoCal piece and Chris Hoene op-ed for the strongest No case, and any strong Yes case I might be missing (e.g., from the Howard Jarvis commentary in CalMatters).

Also — I should check whether there's a concern that Prop 43 could interact with other 2026 props. E.g., Prop 41 (audits/spending limits for special taxes) and Prop 42. Probably not directly.

AGAINST (NO):
1. Anti-majoritarian: entrenches a supermajority requirement, letting ~34% of voters block what 66% support. It permanently writes into the constitution a restriction on the initiative power — one of the few checks on legislatures. Constitutional amendment: the Legislature can't fix it later; only voters can.
2. It's a permanent, one-way ratchet toward Prop 13's already-dysfunctional structure — at exactly the moment California faces ~$30B/yr in federal Medi-Cal cuts from H.R. 1 and local governments face rising costs (wildfire, homelessness, infrastructure). The state and locals have extremely constrained revenue tools; Prop 43 removes one of the few remaining ones.
3. Perverse incentives: After Prop 43, dedicated/earmarked (more accountable, more transparent) taxes need two-thirds, while unrestricted general taxes need only a majority. So Prop 43 pushes communities toward less-accountable general taxes. Both SPUR and even the Mercury News (which endorsed YES) acknowledge this is "backwards."
4. Undisclosed second provision: subdivision (b) bans all voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes. The LAO's analysis, the official title/summary, and neither ballot argument mention it. That's a meaningful hidden change — it permanently forecloses, e.g., a future voter initiative to tax commercial property at value (split-roll style) or any value-based property tax. Voting YES on a constitutional amendment whose operative provisions are not described in the ballot materials is a transparency problem.
5. Real-world casualties: documented measures that would have failed — LA Measure ULA (58%, raised $1.4B for affordable housing/homelessness), SF Prop C (61%, homelessness services), SF Prop G (60.76%, teacher pay), Fresno Measure P (52%, parks), Sonoma County fire/wildfire sales tax (62%, 2024), Alameda County hospital parcel tax (64.7%, 2025), Santa Clara Valley Open Space Authority Measure D (55%, wildfire/flood/open space, 2026), Madera County transportation sales tax (52%, 2024). Many of these are exactly the services Californians say they want: wildfire response, hospitals, teachers, housing.
6. Who's behind it and who benefits: Yes campaign ~$14M, with ~$9.9M from the California Business Roundtable Issues PAC (top donors Peter Thiel, Kim DeGeorge) plus $1M each from Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett (large real estate owners). The measure originated as a real-estate industry campaign against LA's mansion tax. The "taxpayer protection" framing is largely funded by the corporate taxpayers who'd be protected. Meanwhile, the measure's own author (Buffy Wicks) and the Governor who brokered the deal (Newsom) now oppose it. The Legislature passed it 68–2 / 35–1 not as an endorsement of policy but as a hostage trade to kill a far worse retroactive initiative — and the Yes campaign's argument touts that near-unanimous vote as evidence of merit, which is misleading.
7. The Yes argument contains claims not supported by the measure: "over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade" (most weren't citizen-initiated special taxes, the only kind affected); "protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes" / "some cities charge transfer taxes as high as 6%" (Prop 43 does NOT cap transfer taxes — the withdrawn initiative did); "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" (already true for special taxes; Prop 43 adds no enforcement). So the official argument materially overstates what the measure does.
8. It doesn't lower anyone's taxes. It's purely a future procedural constraint.
9. Even the pro-43 Mercury News editorial frames the correct solution as holistic reform of Prop 13 decided by voters — yet Prop 43 moves in the opposite direction, making the structure more rigid. The Santa Cruz Sentinel board was divided and recommended NO, saying the debate "should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal."
10. Editorial/organizational balance: NO — Sacramento Bee/McClatchy boards, LA Times (Skelton: no), LWV California, ACLU SoCal, SPUR, CA Democratic Party, firefighters, teachers, nurses, Cal Cities/League of California Cities, CSDA, cities of Berkeley and West Hollywood, Press Democrat, Santa Barbara Independent, George Skelton. YES — Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, Daily Bulletin/Southern California News Group, Howard Jarvis, Reform California, CA Republican Party, CalTax, CA Small Business Association, CA Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, Family Business Assn.
11. Polling: PPIC Oct: 42% yes / 55% no; IGS/LAT Oct: 36% yes / 46% no. Voters trend against it as they learn about it.

Counter-consideration for YES: Is the "sham initiative" problem serious enough to justify permanently restricting the initiative power? I think the answer is that the problem is real but is better solved by targeted anti-evasion legislation (e.g., rules barring government-official-sponsored initiatives, as courts already scrutinize) rather than a constitutional supermajority requirement that applies to all genuine grassroots initiatives too. Also note: California already has two-thirds for government-proposed special taxes, and Prop 43 wouldn't change that. The initiative path is the only escape valve, and it's the one designed for exactly the case where elected officials won't act.

Also, note the asymmetry: The two-thirds rule for government-proposed special taxes came from Prop 13/62/218 — voter-approved. Extending it to initiatives is arguably "restoring voter intent." But the courts held that the initiative power is reserved and restrictions must be explicit; and voters have repeatedly rejected expanding Prop 13-style limits (e.g., they killed split-roll... no wait, they killed Prop 15 in 2020 which would have loosened Prop 13; and they killed the 2024 Taxpayer Protection Act via court). Hmm — actually the courts removed the 2024 measure, so voters never got to vote. And voters approved Prop 13, 62, 218 — so on balance, California voters have historically supported tax-limiting measures. But those all applied to government-proposed taxes.

One more consideration: the "majority rule" principle vs. "supermajority for taxes." Many democracies require supermajorities for tax increases at the legislative level. But here it's the voters themselves voting. Restricting what a majority of voters can decide is a serious limitation on popular sovereignty, permanently entrenched in the constitution.

Another consideration: does Prop 43 apply to school district parcel taxes? Parcel taxes for school districts: currently, school district parcel taxes require 55% under Proposition 39? No — Prop 39 (2000) is for GO bonds at 55%. School parcel taxes require two-thirds under Art XIII C (they're special taxes) when placed by the district; when placed by initiative, majority. Hmm, actually school parcel taxes are almost always placed by the district, requiring two-thirds. So Prop 43 mostly affects citizen initiatives.

Important: For special districts, ALL taxes are special taxes (per Art XIII C §1(d)). So Prop 43 means any voter-initiated tax for a special district needs two-thirds. That includes fire districts, transit districts, hospital districts, open space districts. That's a significant constraint.

Also note the LAO's analysis omitted subdivision (b) entirely. That's a notable gap.

Also let me check the ACLU SoCal piece and Chris Hoene op-ed for the strongest No case, and any strong Yes case I might be missing (e.g., from the Howard Jarvis commentary in CalMatters).

Also — I should check whether there's a concern that Prop 43 could interact with other 2026 props. E.g., Prop 41 (audits/spending limits for special taxes) and Prop 42. Probably not directly.

# 2026 California Proposition 43
**Proposition 43** is a proposed legislative constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.
Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under Proposition 13 for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local initiative power.^[1]^ Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the California Constitution.^[2]^
Proposition 43 was proposed to overturn appellate court rulings following the 2017 *Upland* decision by the California Supreme Court,^[3]^ which created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13.
These appellate court rulings held that citizen-led special tax proposals under the local initiative power were no longer subject to the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13.

Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. The opposing view: A city councilmember from Sonoma believes Prop. 43 enables minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/), making it harder to fund vital government functions . Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

Photo by Florence Middleton, CalMatters This story is part of California Voices, a commentary forum aiming to broaden our understanding of the state and spotlight Californians directly impacted by policy or its absence. Learn more here (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/). California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) that the courts muddied. Guest Commentary written by Sandra Lowe Sandra Lowe is a member of the Sonoma City Council and a longtime political consultant. Sometimes things that sound simple are not. Let’s take Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/). Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments’ decisions: majority rule. Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority. Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected. In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H (https://sonomacounty.gov/administrative-support-and-fiscal-services/county-executives-office/strategic-initiatives/fire-services-project/measure-h) in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee. Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote (https://ballotpedia.org/Sonoma_County,_California,_Measure_H,_Fire_Prevention_and_Disaster_Response_Sales_Tax_Measure_(March_2024)). READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) California courts muddied tax rules set by voters. Proposition 43 cleans up their mistake (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders. No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent. Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions. The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding (https://health.alamedacountyca.gov/program/measures-a-c-and-w/) and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation (https://www.openspaceauthority.org/whats-new/press-release-measure-d). Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime. Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let’s not go backward. Read more from CalMatters Text Get breaking news on your phone. Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

# Proposition 43
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
### Fiscal Effects
***Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future.*** Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes.
As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be.
The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

3. 2026 California Proposition 43
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_43
**Proposition 43** is a proposed legislative constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.
Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under Proposition 13 for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local initiative power.^[1]^ Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the California Constitution.^[2]^
Proposition 43 was proposed to overturn appellate court rulings following the 2017 *Upland* decision by the California Supreme Court,^[3]^ which created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13.
These appellate court rulings held that citizen-led special tax proposals under the local initiative power were no longer subject to the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13.

Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

***Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future.*** Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes.
As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be.
The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.

A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
### Fiscal Effects
***Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future.*** Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes.
As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be.
The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Supporters of Proposition 43 Include:19
• Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association20
• California Taxpayers Association
• California Small Business Association
• Family Business Association of California
• California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
• Reform California21
• California Republican Party
The proponents’ official website is “Yes on 43: Taxpayer
Protection,” https://yesonprop43.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised a total of
$14,856,760.22
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difficult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.
SUPPORT FOR PROPOSITION 43
Opponents of Proposition 43 Include:24
• California Democratic Party25
• State Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14)26
• Evolve California27
• Sierra Business Council
• California Professional Firefighters
• Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
• California School Employees Association
• California State Association of Counties
• League of Women Voters of California
• California Teachers Association
The opponents’ official website is “No on 43,”
https://www.noprop43ca.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, opponents had raised a total of
$4,864,393.28
Opponents argue that Proposition 43 would:29
• Threaten funding for parks, affordable housing, firefight-
ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local
revenue.30
• Make it more difficult for cities to secure future revenue
measures.31
• Make California “the hardest place in the country” to raise
local revenue.32
• Undermine majority rule by empowering a minority to
block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 43
A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.
A YES VOTE ON PROPOSITION 43 A NO VOTE ON PROPOSITION 43

SUBJECT: Recommendation to Oppose Proposition 43, Limits Voter’s Ability to Raise
