RECOMMENDATION
Berkeley City Council adopt a resolution opposing Proposition 43, a constitutional amendment
on the November 2026 statewide ballot to limit voter's ability to raise revenues for local
government services.
Summary:
Proposition 43 is a legislatively proposed constitutional amendment (ACA 22) that would change
the voter-approval requirements for local special taxes and will appear before voters at the
November 3, 2026, statewide general election.
Beginning January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would require all local special taxes to receive
approval from two-thirds of the voters voting on the tax, regardless of whether the measure is
placed on the ballot by a local governing body or through the local initiative process.
The measure would also prohibit a local government, including its electorate acting through the
initiative power, from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property except as permitted under
existing constitutional provisions.
Ballot Description:
Proposition 43 would add Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution and make
the following changes to local taxation authority:
Two-Thirds Requirement for All Local Special Taxes
Beginning January 1, 2027, a local government, including the electorate of a local
government exercising the initiative power, could not impose, extend, or increase a
special tax unless the tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
Local government-sponsored special taxes are already subject to two-thirds voter
approval under Article XIII C. Proposition 43 would extend that same threshold to
special taxes proposed through the voter initiative process, reversing the current judicial
interpretation that permits those measures to pass with a simple majority.
Ad Valorem Property Tax Limitation
Proposition 43 would prohibit a local government, including its electorate acting through
the initiative power, from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property except as
authorized by paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D of the
California Constitution. This provision clarifies that the existing constitutional limitation
applies to both local governing bodies and local voters acting by initiative.
Prospective Application
The measure would operate prospectively, applying to voter-proposed ballot measures
approved after January 1, 2027.
BACKGROUND:
Proposition 13 and Local Tax Approval Requirements
California's modern local tax framework largely stems from Proposition 131, approved by voters
in 1978. Proposition 13 limited property tax rates and established voter approval requirements
for local taxes. Specifically, it capped the general ad valorem property tax rate at 1 percent of
assessed value, limited annual increases in assessed value, and required two-thirds voter approval
for cities, counties, and special districts to impose special taxes.
Proposition 218, approved by voters in 1996, added Articles XIII C and XIII D to the California
Constitution. Under Article XIII C, local governments may not impose, extend, or increase a
special tax without approval by two-thirds of voters. A special tax is defined as any tax imposed
for a specific purpose rather than for general governmental use.
Article XIII C also classifies local taxes as either general or special. General taxes used for
general governmental purposes generally require majority voter approval. When proposed by a
local governing body, a general tax must generally appear on the ballot at a regularly scheduled
general election for members of that governing body, unless an emergency is declared by a
unanimous vote.
Article XIII C also expressly preserves the voters' initiative power to reduce or repeal local taxes,
assessments, fees, and charges. More broadly, Article II of the California Constitution reserves
the initiative power to the people, and courts have traditionally construed that power broadly.
Court Decisions Affecting Initiative Taxes
Recent court decisions have interpreted these constitutional provisions differently when taxes are
proposed through the citizen initiative process rather than by a local government.
California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland
California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017) 3 Cal.5th 924 arose from a local
initiative to repeal the city's ban on medical marijuana dispensaries, and impose an
annual $75,000 licensing and inspection charge. The City of Upland concluded that
1 California Proposition 43, Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and
Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment (2026) - Ballotpedia
because the charge exceeded estimated regulatory costs, it would operate as a general tax
and had to appear at a regularly scheduled general election rather than the special election
requested by the proponents.
The California Supreme Court held that Article XIII C's election-timing requirement
applied to taxes imposed by a 'local government' and did not clearly restrict voters acting
through the initiative power. The requirement therefore did not apply to the voter-
sponsored initiative. Upland addressed election timing for a voter-initiated general tax,
not the approval threshold for a voter-initiated special tax.
San Francisco Proposition C and the Current Majority Threshold
Following Upland, the Court of Appeal in City and County of San Francisco v. All
Persons Interested in the Matter of Proposition C (2020) 51 Cal.App.5th 703 held that a
voter-initiated local special tax may be approved by a simple majority rather than two-
thirds of voters. The California Supreme Court declined review. Subsequent appellate
decisions followed the same approach, allowing several voter-initiated local special taxes
to take effect with majority approval.
Under current law, the approval threshold for a local special tax therefore depends on how the
measure reaches the ballot. A governing-body-sponsored special tax requires two-thirds voter
approval, while a voter-initiated special tax may pass with a majority. Proposition 43 would
eliminate that distinction by applying the two-thirds threshold to both.
ACA 13 (Ward)
In 2023, the League of California Cities supported ACA 13 a constitutional amendment dealing
with voter thresholds. The measure would have required any state or local initiative measure to
conform with any increased voter threshold that it seeks to impose on future ballot measures. For
example, if a measure looks to increase the voter threshold of general tax measures from a
simple majority (50% +1) to a supermajority (2/3), the measure would be required to pass by that
same supermajority.
The measure would have also preserved the right of local governments to place advisory
questions on the ballot to ask voters their opinion on the issue.
ACA 13 also stated that the provisions of this constitutional amendment apply to all statewide
initiative measures submitted to voters on or after January 1, 2024. It contained intent language
stating that the provisions of this measure are not intended to reverse or invalidate provisions of
the California Constitution in effect before January 1, 2024, including the provisions of
Proposition 13 of 1978.
ACA 13 was originally scheduled to be on the March 2024 ballot, but was subsequently moved
to the November 2024 ballot, and then again to the November 2026 ballot.
The 2026 Ballot Agreement
ACA 22, the legislation to place Proposition 43 on the November ballot, is the product of an
agreement between state leaders and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA). In
exchange for the Legislature passing ACA 22 and removing ACA 13 from the November ballot,
HJTA withdrew its Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Initiative 25-
0006A1). The proposal included a two-thirds requirement for all local special taxes, restrictions
on real property transfer taxes, and the invalidation of certain existing taxes. The League of
California Cities opposed the measure based on its effects on existing voter-approved revenues,
local taxation authority, and essential local services.
Proposition 43 would operate prospectively and would not repeal or reduce existing real property
transfer taxes, invalidate existing voter-approved special taxes, limit documentary transfer tax
rates, or create a deadline for local governments to eliminate existing taxes. The result is a new
constitutional restriction on future local revenue measures by requiring two-thirds approval for
voter-initiated special taxes that may pass by majority vote under current law.
Proposition 43 Fiscal Impact:
Proposition 43 would not directly reduce or eliminate existing city revenues. Current real
property transfer taxes, parcel taxes, and other voter-initiated special taxes would remain in
effect. Its fiscal effects would instead arise when future voter-initiated special taxes receive
majority support but fall short of the new two-thirds threshold.
The statewide amount of foregone revenue cannot be reliably estimated because it would depend
on the number, structure, tax base, and election results of future local measures.
Existing voter-initiated special taxes illustrate the potential scale of revenue that could be
affected if comparable measures are proposed after January 1, 2027. Examples of existing taxes
that passed with less than two-thirds support include:
● Los Angeles Measure ULA: approximately $655 million to $1.2 billion annually.
● Santa Monica Measure GS: approximately $54 million annually.
● Oakland Measure AA: approximately $30 million to $36 million annually.
● Berkeley Measure FF: approximately $15 million annually.
Proposition 43 would not invalidate or reduce revenue from these existing measures. However, a
future measure with the same level of voter support would not take effect unless it received two-
thirds approval. These examples are therefore illustrative of the type and magnitude of future
locally dedicated revenue that could be foregone, not an estimate of an immediate revenue loss
under the measure
Additionally, Proposition 43 may also influence how future revenue measures are structured.
Communities may favor general taxes, which remain subject to majority approval, over special
taxes dedicated to specific purposes. Although this may preserve a path to revenue, it would
prevent voters from legally restricting the funds to the program identified in the measure and
could place additional demands on a city's general fund.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS:
Opposing Proposition 43 has no financial implications for the City of Berkeley.

RESOLUTION TO OPPOSE PROPOSITION 43:
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES
FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES
WHEREAS, communities across California have been coming together to pass local ballot
measures to provide critical funding for fire and wildfire prevention, local roads, libraries and
parks as well as housing and alleviating homelessness; and
WHEREAS, Proposition 43 on the November 3, 2026 statewide ballot limits voters’ ability to
raise revenues to fund local services; and
WHEREAS, beginning January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would raise the percentage of votes
needed to approve any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by the voters;
and
WHEREAS, under Proposition 43, when voters place measures on the ballot to fund specific
local services, opponents would only need one-third (33.4%) of the vote to block it; and
WHEREAS, if Proposition 43 had been the law, California communities would not have been
able to raise nearly $3 billion in revenue every year that funds firefighters and 911 response,
childcare, homelessness solutions, street repairs, parks and libraries; and
WHEREAS, Proposition 43 does not cut taxes. It limits local voters’ power to raise revenue to
fund local services; and
WHEREAS, the measure is opposed by a broad coalition of local governments, including the
League of California Cities, nurses, teachers and school employees, firefighters, and law
enforcement; and
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Berkeley City Council opposes Proposition 43 on
the November 2026 statewide ballot; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that we direct staff to email a copy of this adopted resolution
to the League of California Cities at BallotMeasures@calcities.org.

measure reaches the ballot. A governing-body-sponsored special tax requires two-thirds voter
approval, while a voter-initiated special tax may pass with a majority. Proposition 43 would
eliminate that distinction by applying the two-thirds threshold to both.
ACA 13 (Ward)
In 2023, the League of California Cities supported ACA 13 a constitutional amendment dealing
with voter thresholds. The measure would have required any state or local initiative measure to
conform with any increased voter threshold that it seeks to impose on future ballot measures. For
example, if a measure looks to increase the voter threshold of general tax measures from a
simple majority (50% +1) to a supermajority (2/3), the measure would be required to pass by that
same supermajority.
The measure would have also preserved the right of local governments to place advisory
questions on the ballot to ask voters their opinion on the issue.
ACA 13 also stated that the provisions of this constitutional amendment apply to all statewide
initiative measures submitted to voters on or after January 1, 2024. It contained intent language
stating that the provisions of this measure are not intended to reverse or invalidate provisions of
the California Constitution in effect before January 1, 2024, including the provisions of
Proposition 13 of 1978.
ACA 13 was originally scheduled to be on the March 2024 ballot, but was subsequently moved
to the November 2024 ballot, and then again to the November 2026 ballot.
The 2026 Ballot Agreement
ACA 22, the legislation to place Proposition 43 on the November ballot, is the product of an
agreement between state leaders and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA). In
exchange for the Legislature passing ACA 22 and removing ACA 13 from the November ballot,
HJTA withdrew its Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Initiative 25-
0006A1). The proposal included a two-thirds requirement for all local special taxes, restrictions
on real property transfer taxes, and the invalidation of certain existing taxes. The League of
California Cities opposed the measure based on its effects on existing voter-approved revenues,
local taxation authority, and essential local services.
Proposition 43 would operate prospectively and would not repeal or reduce existing real property
transfer taxes, invalidate existing voter-approved special taxes, limit documentary transfer tax
rates, or create a deadline for local governments to eliminate existing taxes. The result is a new
constitutional restriction on future local revenue measures by requiring two-thirds approval for
voter-initiated special taxes that may pass by majority vote under current law.
Proposition 43 Fiscal Impact:
Proposition 43 would not directly reduce or eliminate existing city revenues. Current real
property transfer taxes, parcel taxes, and other voter-initiated special taxes would remain in
effect. Its fiscal effects would instead arise when future voter-initiated special taxes receive
majority support but fall short of the new two-thirds threshold.
The statewide amount of foregone revenue cannot be reliably estimated because it would depend
on the number, structure, tax base, and election results of future local measures.
Existing voter-initiated special taxes illustrate the potential scale of revenue that could be
affected if comparable measures are proposed after January 1, 2027. Examples of existing taxes
that passed with less than two-thirds support include:
● Los Angeles Measure ULA: approximately $655 million to $1.2 billion annually.
● Santa Monica Measure GS: approximately $54 million annually.
● Oakland Measure AA: approximately $30 million to $36 million annually.
● Berkeley Measure FF: approximately $15 million annually.
Proposition 43 would not invalidate or reduce revenue from these existing measures. However, a
future measure with the same level of voter support would not take effect unless it received two-
thirds approval. These examples are therefore illustrative of the type and magnitude of future
locally dedicated revenue that could be foregone, not an estimate of an immediate revenue loss
under the measure
Additionally, Proposition 43 may also influence how future revenue measures are structured.
Communities may favor general taxes, which remain subject to majority approval, over special
taxes dedicated to specific purposes. Although this may preserve a path to revenue, it would
prevent voters from legally restricting the funds to the program identified in the measure and
could place additional demands on a city's general fund.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS:
Opposing Proposition 43 has no financial implications for the City of Berkeley.

RESOLUTION TO OPPOSE PROPOSITION 43:
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES
FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES
WHEREAS, communities across California have been coming together to pass local ballot
measures to provide critical funding for fire and wildfire prevention, local roads, libraries and
parks as well as housing and alleviating homelessness; and
WHEREAS, Proposition 43 on the November 3, 2026 statewide ballot limits voters’ ability to
raise revenues to fund local services; and
WHEREAS, beginning January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would raise the percentage of votes
needed to approve any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by the voters;
and
WHEREAS, under Proposition 43, when voters place measures on the ballot to fund specific
local services, opponents would only need one-third (33.4%) of the vote to block it; and
WHEREAS, if Proposition 43 had been the law, California communities would not have been
able to raise nearly $3 billion in revenue every year that funds firefighters and 911 response,
childcare, homelessness solutions, street repairs, parks and libraries; and
WHEREAS, Proposition 43 does not cut taxes. It limits local voters’ power to raise revenue to
fund local services; and
WHEREAS, the measure is opposed by a broad coalition of local governments, including the
League of California Cities, nurses, teachers and school employees, firefighters, and law
enforcement; and
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Berkeley City Council opposes Proposition 43 on
the November 2026 statewide ballot; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that we direct staff to email a copy of this adopted resolution
to the League of California Cities at BallotMeasures@calcities.org.

governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.

majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June

state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative

and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16

Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

September 29, 2026
TO: Honorable Berkeley City City Councilmembers
FROM: Mayor Adena Ishii (Author), Councilmember Lunaparra (Co-Sponsor),
Councilmember Blackaby (Co-Sponsor), Councilmember Tregub (Co-Sponsor)
SUBJECT: Recommendation to Oppose Proposition 43, Limits Voter’s Ability to Raise
Revenues for Local Government Services
RECOMMENDATION
Berkeley City Council adopt a resolution opposing Proposition 43, a constitutional amendment
on the November 2026 statewide ballot to limit voter's ability to raise revenues for local
government services.
Summary:
Proposition 43 is a legislatively proposed constitutional amendment (ACA 22) that would change
the voter-approval requirements for local special taxes and will appear before voters at the
November 3, 2026, statewide general election.
Beginning January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would require all local special taxes to receive
approval from two-thirds of the voters voting on the tax, regardless of whether the measure is
placed on the ballot by a local governing body or through the local initiative process.
The measure would also prohibit a local government, including its electorate acting through the
initiative power, from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property except as permitted under
existing constitutional provisions.
Ballot Description:
Proposition 43 would add Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution and make
the following changes to local taxation authority:
Two-Thirds Requirement for All Local Special Taxes
Beginning January 1, 2027, a local government, including the electorate of a local
government exercising the initiative power, could not impose, extend, or increase a
special tax unless the tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
Local government-sponsored special taxes are already subject to two-thirds voter
approval under Article XIII C. Proposition 43 would extend that same threshold to
special taxes proposed through the voter initiative process, reversing the current judicial
interpretation that permits those measures to pass with a simple majority.
Ad Valorem Property Tax Limitation
Proposition 43 would prohibit a local government, including its electorate acting through
the initiative power, from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property except as
authorized by paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D of the
California Constitution. This provision clarifies that the existing constitutional limitation
applies to both local governing bodies and local voters acting by initiative.
Prospective Application
The measure would operate prospectively, applying to voter-proposed ballot measures
approved after January 1, 2027.
BACKGROUND:
Proposition 13 and Local Tax Approval Requirements
California's modern local tax framework largely stems from Proposition 131, approved by voters
in 1978. Proposition 13 limited property tax rates and established voter approval requirements
for local taxes. Specifically, it capped the general ad valorem property tax rate at 1 percent of
assessed value, limited annual increases in assessed value, and required two-thirds voter approval
for cities, counties, and special districts to impose special taxes.
Proposition 218, approved by voters in 1996, added Articles XIII C and XIII D to the California
Constitution. Under Article XIII C, local governments may not impose, extend, or increase a
special tax without approval by two-thirds of voters. A special tax is defined as any tax imposed
for a specific purpose rather than for general governmental use.
Article XIII C also classifies local taxes as either general or special. General taxes used for
general governmental purposes generally require majority voter approval. When proposed by a
local governing body, a general tax must generally appear on the ballot at a regularly scheduled
general election for members of that governing body, unless an emergency is declared by a
unanimous vote.
Article XIII C also expressly preserves the voters' initiative power to reduce or repeal local taxes,
assessments, fees, and charges. More broadly, Article II of the California Constitution reserves
the initiative power to the people, and courts have traditionally construed that power broadly.
Court Decisions Affecting Initiative Taxes
Recent court decisions have interpreted these constitutional provisions differently when taxes are
proposed through the citizen initiative process rather than by a local government.
California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland
California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017) 3 Cal.5th 924 arose from a local
initiative to repeal the city's ban on medical marijuana dispensaries, and impose an
annual $75,000 licensing and inspection charge. The City of Upland concluded that
1 California Proposition 43, Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and
Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment (2026) - Ballotpedia
because the charge exceeded estimated regulatory costs, it would operate as a general tax
and had to appear at a regularly scheduled general election rather than the special election
requested by the proponents.
The California Supreme Court held that Article XIII C's election-timing requirement
applied to taxes imposed by a 'local government' and did not clearly restrict voters acting
through the initiative power. The requirement therefore did not apply to the voter-
sponsored initiative. Upland addressed election timing for a voter-initiated general tax,
not the approval threshold for a voter-initiated special tax.
San Francisco Proposition C and the Current Majority Threshold
Following Upland, the Court of Appeal in City and County of San Francisco v. All
Persons Interested in the Matter of Proposition C (2020) 51 Cal.App.5th 703 held that a
voter-initiated local special tax may be approved by a simple majority rather than two-
thirds of voters. The California Supreme Court declined review. Subsequent appellate
decisions followed the same approach, allowing several voter-initiated local special taxes
to take effect with majority approval.
Under current law, the approval threshold for a local special tax therefore depends on how the
measure reaches the ballot. A governing-body-sponsored special tax requires two-thirds voter
approval, while a voter-initiated special tax may pass with a majority. Proposition 43 would
eliminate that distinction by applying the two-thirds threshold to both.
ACA 13 (Ward)
In 2023, the League of California Cities supported ACA 13 a constitutional amendment dealing
with voter thresholds. The measure would have required any state or local initiative measure to
conform with any increased voter threshold that it seeks to impose on future ballot measures. For
example, if a measure looks to increase the voter threshold of general tax measures from a
simple majority (50% +1) to a supermajority (2/3), the measure would be required to pass by that
same supermajority.
The measure would have also preserved the right of local governments to place advisory
questions on the ballot to ask voters their opinion on the issue.
ACA 13 also stated that the provisions of this constitutional amendment apply to all statewide
initiative measures submitted to voters on or after January 1, 2024. It contained intent language
stating that the provisions of this measure are not intended to reverse or invalidate provisions of
the California Constitution in effect before January 1, 2024, including the provisions of
Proposition 13 of 1978.
ACA 13 was originally scheduled to be on the March 2024 ballot, but was subsequently moved
to the November 2024 ballot, and then again to the November 2026 ballot.
The 2026 Ballot Agreement
ACA 22, the legislation to place Proposition 43 on the November ballot, is the product of an
agreement between state leaders and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA). In
exchange for the Legislature passing ACA 22 and removing ACA 13 from the November ballot,
HJTA withdrew its Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Initiative 25-
0006A1). The proposal included a two-thirds requirement for all local special taxes, restrictions
on real property transfer taxes, and the invalidation of certain existing taxes. The League of
California Cities opposed the measure based on its effects on existing voter-approved revenues,
local taxation authority, and essential local services.
Proposition 43 would operate prospectively and would not repeal or reduce existing real property
transfer taxes, invalidate existing voter-approved special taxes, limit documentary transfer tax
rates, or create a deadline for local governments to eliminate existing taxes. The result is a new
constitutional restriction on future local revenue measures by requiring two-thirds approval for
voter-initiated special taxes that may pass by majority vote under current law.
Proposition 43 Fiscal Impact:
Proposition 43 would not directly reduce or eliminate existing city revenues. Current real
property transfer taxes, parcel taxes, and other voter-initiated special taxes would remain in
effect. Its fiscal effects would instead arise when future voter-initiated special taxes receive
majority support but fall short of the new two-thirds threshold.
The statewide amount of foregone revenue cannot be reliably estimated because it would depend
on the number, structure, tax base, and election results of future local measures.
Existing voter-initiated special taxes illustrate the potential scale of revenue that could be
affected if comparable measures are proposed after January 1, 2027. Examples of existing taxes
that passed with less than two-thirds support include:
● Los Angeles Measure ULA: approximately $655 million to $1.2 billion annually.
● Santa Monica Measure GS: approximately $54 million annually.
● Oakland Measure AA: approximately $30 million to $36 million annually.
● Berkeley Measure FF: approximately $15 million annually.
Proposition 43 would not invalidate or reduce revenue from these existing measures. However, a
future measure with the same level of voter support would not take effect unless it received two-
thirds approval. These examples are therefore illustrative of the type and magnitude of future
locally dedicated revenue that could be foregone, not an estimate of an immediate revenue loss
under the measure
Additionally, Proposition 43 may also influence how future revenue measures are structured.
Communities may favor general taxes, which remain subject to majority approval, over special
taxes dedicated to specific purposes. Although this may preserve a path to revenue, it would
prevent voters from legally restricting the funds to the program identified in the measure and
could place additional demands on a city's general fund.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS:
Opposing Proposition 43 has no financial implications for the City of Berkeley.

PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters

the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

I now have a comprehensive picture. One more important legal-historical fact from the CMC backgrounder: In June 2024, the California Supreme Court UNANIMOUSLY ruled that a very similar measure (the Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act, backed by HJTA and California Business Roundtable) would have been an invalid constitutional REVISION — "based on its far-reaching changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the state and local levels." 

That's an important data point: the state's highest court concluded that a sweeping change to local revenue processes of this kind goes beyond what can be done by simple amendment. Prop 43 (ACA 22) is narrower and is a legislatively-referred constitutional amendment — the Legislature CAN propose revisions via a constitutional convention, but ACA 22 is an amendment placed by two-thirds legislative vote. Actually the Legislature can place amendments on the ballot with 2/3 vote (Art XVIII §1); revisions require a constitutional convention (Art XVIII §2), though the Legislature can also propose... Actually Article XVIII Section 2 says the Legislature may submit at a general election the question whether to call a convention to revise the Constitution. So the Legislature can't directly propose a revision either.

Anyway, the 2024 ruling (Legislature v. Weber) suggests that Prop 43, while narrower, is in the same direction as a change the court found constitutionally impermissible by initiative. Prop 43's narrower scope is presumably designed to fit within "amendment" rather than "revision."

This is relevant: it shows the courts viewed the broad version as an unconstitutional aggrandizement. Prop 43 is a scaled-back version.

Now let me weigh everything and reach a decision.

Let me also quickly check: is there anything about the effect of Prop 43 on local measures that voters might otherwise use to LIMIT or repeal taxes? Art XIII C §3 expressly preserves the initiative power to reduce or repeal taxes/fees. Prop 43's §4.5(a) says "no local government, including the electorate... may impose, extend, or increase any special tax... unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote." A repeal isn't imposing/extending/increasing. So repeals still by majority. Good — it's not asymmetric in that way.

However, there IS an asymmetry in another sense: raising the threshold for special taxes makes it harder to ADD revenue but existing revenue streams are protected (locked in), and renewals of expiring taxes require two-thirds. Many existing voter-initiated special taxes have sunset dates. Renewal would need two-thirds. E.g., Sonoma Measure H, Alameda Measure B (hospital parcel tax). So Prop 43 does put existing expiring taxes at risk on renewal. Berkeley's report notes this.

Actually, wait: Does the two-thirds rule already apply to renewals placed by the governing body? Yes. So for council-placed renewals, two-thirds already. For initiative renewals, it changes.

Let me think about the bottom line now.

Framework for decision: The question is "What should I vote on this prop?" I should give a yes or no answer with reasoning.

Arguments weighing:

MERITS OF YES:
- Internal consistency of the tax framework. Two identical taxes shouldn't have different thresholds based on procedural route. This is a genuine anomaly, court-created, not voter-created.
- Real abuse documented: governments and interested parties manufacturing "citizen initiatives" to cut the threshold in half. That's a legitimate integrity problem.
- Prospective only; doesn't repeal existing taxes; doesn't touch general taxes; much narrower than the withdrawn initiative (which would have cost locals up to $2B/yr and voided existing taxes).
- Earmarked taxes lock money for decades, reducing fiscal flexibility; a supermajority for earmarking is defensible.

MERITS OF NO:
- Permanent constitutional entrenchment of an anti-majoritarian rule restricting the initiative power — one of the few remaining tools for Californians to act when elected officials won't. And it's a one-way ratchet: the Legislature can never fix it.
- Timing/context is terrible: California faces ~$30B/year in federal Medi-Cal cuts (H.R. 1, effective Jan 1, 2027 — the exact same date Prop 43 kicks in), rising wildfire costs, housing crisis. Prop 43 removes a key local revenue tool at exactly that moment.
- Perverse incentive: after Prop 43, unrestricted general taxes remain majority-approvable while dedicated, earmarked, accountable special taxes require two-thirds. So Prop 43 pushes communities toward LESS accountable taxes. Even the pro-43 Mercury News board called the underlying structure "backwards" — Prop 43 locks that backwards structure deeper.
- Undisclosed provision: subdivision (b) permanently bans voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes. Not mentioned in the official title/summary, the LAO analysis, or either ballot argument. Voting YES on a constitutional amendment with an operative provision that no official ballot material describes is a real transparency problem — and it forecloses future value-based property tax reform (e.g., split-roll style measures) by initiative forever.
- The official YES argument materially overstates: claims about "2,000 new taxes," "6% real estate transfer taxes," and "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" — Prop 43 does not cap transfer taxes and adds no new spending-enforcement mechanism. It's arguing for a different (withdrawn) measure.
- Who benefits / who pays: Yes campaign ~$14.9M, with ~$9.9M from the California Business Roundtable Issues PAC (top donors incl. Peter Thiel), plus $1M each from Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett. The measure's origin was the real estate industry's campaign against LA's Measure ULA. It's framed as "taxpayer protection" but is funded by the largest taxpayers it would shield.

# Vote **NO** on Proposition 43

## What it actually is
Prop 43 (ACA 22, Res. Ch. 132, Statutes of 2026) adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution — the article created by Prop 13. Effective **January 1, 2027**, it does two things:

1. **(a)** Any local **special tax** (money earmarked for a specific purpose) proposed by citizen initiative must now win **two-thirds** instead of a simple majority — reversing the *Upland* (2017) line of appellate rulings (SF Prop C 2020, Fresno 2020, *HJTA v. SF* 2021).
2. **(b)** Permanently **bans** local governments *and voters acting by initiative* from imposing **ad valorem (value-based) property taxes**, except as Art. XIII D allows.

It was placed on the ballot June 25, 2026 (Assembly 68–2, Senate 35–1) as a last-minute trade: the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its far more damaging "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13," which would have *retroactively voided* existing taxes and capped transfer taxes (LAO: up to ~$2B/year in local losses), and the Legislature pulled ACA 13 (a "poison pill" requiring supermajority measures to pass by supermajority).

## Why NO

**1. It's a permanent, unfixable restriction on majority rule.** This is a constitutional amendment, so the Legislature can never repair it — only voters can, and Prop 43 makes it harder for voters to act. It writes into the constitution that ~34% of voters can defeat what ~66% want, and it targets specifically the *initiative power*, the one tool designed for when elected officials won't act. Article XIII C expressly preserves the people's reserved power over local taxes; Prop 43 overrides Article II's initiative power "notwithstanding" language.

**2. There's an undisclosed provision.** Subdivision (b) — the ban on voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes — appears **nowhere** in the official title and summary, **nowhere** in the Legislative Analyst's analysis, and in **neither** ballot argument. It would forever foreclose a citizen initiative for a value-based property tax (e.g., a split-roll style commercial property reform). You're being asked to amend the constitution on the basis of materials that describe only half of it.

**3. It's backwards on accountability.** After Prop 43, *unrestricted* general taxes still pass by simple majority, while *dedicated, earmarked* special taxes — the more transparent, more accountable kind voters usually prefer — need two-thirds. It pushes communities toward less-accountable revenue. Even the **Mercury News/East Bay Times**, which endorsed YES, conceded the resulting structure is "backwards" and that real reform must be holistic. The Santa Cruz Sentinel board was divided and recommended NO for exactly that reason.

**4. Terrible timing and real casualties.** It kicks in Jan 1, 2027 — the same date California begins absorbing roughly **$30B/year in federal Medi-Cal cuts** under H.R. 1 — while local governments face wildfire, housing, and infrastructure costs. Measures that won majority support and would have died under this rule:

| Measure | Vote | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| LA Measure ULA (2022) | 57.8% | Affordable housing/homelessness ($1.4B raised) |
| SF Prop C (2018) | 61.3% | Homelessness services |
| SF Prop G (2018) | 60.8% | SFUSD teacher pay |
| Sonoma Measure H (2024) | ~62% | Fire, wildfire, EMS |
| Alameda Measure B (2025) | 64.7% | Washington Hospital parcel tax |
| Santa Clara Open Space Measure D (2026) | 55% | Wildfire/flood prevention, open space |
| Fresno Measure P (2018) | 52.2% | Parks (~$37.5M/yr) |
| Madera Measure T (2024) | 52% | Transportation |

Berkeley's city analysis lists comparable dedicated-revenue streams of $15M–$1.2B annually per city. It also blocks *renewals and increases* of expiring taxes.

**5. Follow the money and the misleading arguments.** The Yes side raised ~$14–15M, including **$9.87M from the California Business Roundtable Issues PAC** (top donors include Peter Thiel) and $1M each from Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett. The whole effort originated in the real estate industry's campaign against LA's mansion tax. The official YES argument also oversells: "2,000 new taxes" mostly weren't citizen-initiated special taxes (the only kind affected); "transfer taxes as high as 6%" are **not** capped by Prop 43 (that was the withdrawn initiative); and "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" is **already law** for special taxes. The No campaign's "$3 billion a year" claim is likewise not an LAO figure — the LAO says the impact is *unknown*.

**6. The near-unanimous legislative vote is not an endorsement.** The YES rebuttal touts it, but the author, **Assemblymember Buffy Wicks**, said days later she is "adamantly opposed" — she wrote it only to kill the retroactive measure. **Gov. Newsom**, who brokered the deal, now calls it "a dangerous corporate power grab." The CA Democratic Party, Becerra, LWV California, League of California Cities, CSAC, California Special Districts Assn., SPUR, ACLU SoCal, CA Professional Firefighters, CTA/CFT, SEIU Nurse Alliance, Cal School Employees Assn., and cities of Berkeley, West Hollywood and San José all oppose. Supporting: HJTA, CalTax, CA Business Roundtable, CA Small Business Assn., Reform California, CA GOP, and editorial boards of the Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, and Southern California News Group. Polling has it losing: PPIC (Oct) **42% yes / 55% no**; IGS–LA Times (Oct) **36% / 46%**.

**7. The courts already flagged this agenda.** In *Legislature v. Weber* (2024), the California Supreme Court **unanimously** removed the same sponsors' broader 2024 measure from the ballot as an invalid constitutional *revision*, citing its "far-reaching changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained." Prop 43 is a scaled-down attempt at the same project.

## The strongest case for YES — and why it doesn't win
The genuine problem is **sham citizen initiatives**: officials and interested parties route their own tax proposals through petition drives purely to halve the passage bar (SF supervisors' 2018 commercial rent tax at 50.8%; the San Diego hotel tax upheld at 65.2% after officials declared it failed; 2026's Measure RTM funded by transit unions/contractors instead of MTC; Oakland Measure E; the Fresno County fight where AB 1923 forced a disputed initiative onto the ballot). Consistency also has real value — identical taxes shouldn't face different thresholds based on procedural routing.

But the remedy is **targeted anti-evasion rules** (courts already scrutinize government-sponsored "initiatives"), not a permanent supermajority requirement that handicaps every authentic grassroots effort too. And Prop 43 doesn't lower anyone's taxes — it only removes one of the last revenue valves in a state whose local tax system Prop 13 already made the most constrained in the country.

**NO.**

# Vote **NO** on Proposition 43

## What it actually is
Prop 43 (ACA 22, Res. Ch. 132, Statutes of 2026) adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution — the article created by Prop 13. Effective **January 1, 2027**, it does two things:

1. **(a)** Any local **special tax** (money earmarked for a specific purpose) proposed by citizen initiative must now win **two-thirds** instead of a simple majority — reversing the *Upland* (2017) line of appellate rulings (SF Prop C 2020, Fresno 2020, *HJTA v. SF* 2021).
2. **(b)** Permanently **bans** local governments *and voters acting by initiative* from imposing **ad valorem (value-based) property taxes**, except as Art. XIII D allows.

It was placed on the ballot June 25, 2026 (Assembly 68–2, Senate 35–1) as a last-minute trade: the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its far more damaging "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13," which would have *retroactively voided* existing taxes and capped transfer taxes (LAO: up to ~$2B/year in local losses), and the Legislature pulled ACA 13 (a "poison pill" requiring supermajority measures to pass by supermajority).

## Why NO

**1. It's a permanent, unfixable restriction on majority rule.** This is a constitutional amendment, so the Legislature can never repair it — only voters can, and Prop 43 makes it harder for voters to act. It writes into the constitution that ~34% of voters can defeat what ~66% want, and it targets specifically the *initiative power*, the one tool designed for when elected officials won't act. Article XIII C expressly preserves the people's reserved power over local taxes; Prop 43 overrides Article II's initiative power "notwithstanding" language.

**2. There's an undisclosed provision.** Subdivision (b) — the ban on voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes — appears **nowhere** in the official title and summary, **nowhere** in the Legislative Analyst's analysis, and in **neither** ballot argument. It would forever foreclose a citizen initiative for a value-based property tax (e.g., a split-roll style commercial property reform). You're being asked to amend the constitution on the basis of materials that describe only half of it.

**3. It's backwards on accountability.** After Prop 43, *unrestricted* general taxes still pass by simple majority, while *dedicated, earmarked* special taxes — the more transparent, more accountable kind voters usually prefer — need two-thirds. It pushes communities toward less-accountable revenue. Even the **Mercury News/East Bay Times**, which endorsed YES, conceded the resulting structure is "backwards" and that real reform must be holistic. The Santa Cruz Sentinel board was divided and recommended NO for exactly that reason.

**4. Terrible timing and real casualties.** It kicks in Jan 1, 2027 — the same date California begins absorbing roughly **$30B/year in federal Medi-Cal cuts** under H.R. 1 — while local governments face wildfire, housing, and infrastructure costs. Measures that won majority support and would have died under this rule:

| Measure | Vote | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| LA Measure ULA (2022) | 57.8% | Affordable housing/homelessness ($1.4B raised) |
| SF Prop C (2018) | 61.3% | Homelessness services |
| SF Prop G (2018) | 60.8% | SFUSD teacher pay |
| Sonoma Measure H (2024) | ~62% | Fire, wildfire, EMS |
| Alameda Measure B (2025) | 64.7% | Washington Hospital parcel tax |
| Santa Clara Open Space Measure D (2026) | 55% | Wildfire/flood prevention, open space |
| Fresno Measure P (2018) | 52.2% | Parks (~$37.5M/yr) |
| Madera Measure T (2024) | 52% | Transportation |

Berkeley's city analysis lists comparable dedicated-revenue streams of $15M–$1.2B annually per city. It also blocks *renewals and increases* of expiring taxes.

**5. Follow the money and the misleading arguments.** The Yes side raised ~$14–15M, including **$9.87M from the California Business Roundtable Issues PAC** (top donors include Peter Thiel) and $1M each from Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett. The whole effort originated in the real estate industry's campaign against LA's mansion tax. The official YES argument also oversells: "2,000 new taxes" mostly weren't citizen-initiated special taxes (the only kind affected); "transfer taxes as high as 6%" are **not** capped by Prop 43 (that was the withdrawn initiative); and "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" is **already law** for special taxes. The No campaign's "$3 billion a year" claim is likewise not an LAO figure — the LAO says the impact is *unknown*.

**6. The near-unanimous legislative vote is not an endorsement.** The YES rebuttal touts it, but the author, **Assemblymember Buffy Wicks**, said days later she is "adamantly opposed" — she wrote it only to kill the retroactive measure. **Gov. Newsom**, who brokered the deal, now calls it "a dangerous corporate power grab." The CA Democratic Party, Becerra, LWV California, League of California Cities, CSAC, California Special Districts Assn., SPUR, ACLU SoCal, CA Professional Firefighters, CTA/CFT, SEIU Nurse Alliance, Cal School Employees Assn., and cities of Berkeley, West Hollywood and San José all oppose. Supporting: HJTA, CalTax, CA Business Roundtable, CA Small Business Assn., Reform California, CA GOP, and editorial boards of the Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, and Southern California News Group. Polling has it losing: PPIC (Oct) **42% yes / 55% no**; IGS–LA Times (Oct) **36% / 46%**.

**7. The courts already flagged this agenda.** In *Legislature v. Weber* (2024), the California Supreme Court **unanimously** removed the same sponsors' broader 2024 measure from the ballot as an invalid constitutional *revision*, citing its "far-reaching changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained." Prop 43 is a scaled-down attempt at the same project.

## The strongest case for YES — and why it doesn't win
The genuine problem is **sham citizen initiatives**: officials and interested parties route their own tax proposals through petition drives purely to halve the passage bar (SF supervisors' 2018 commercial rent tax at 50.8%; the San Diego hotel tax upheld at 65.2% after officials declared it failed; 2026's Measure RTM funded by transit unions/contractors instead of MTC; Oakland Measure E; the Fresno County fight where AB 1923 forced a disputed initiative onto the ballot). Consistency also has real value — identical taxes shouldn't face different thresholds based on procedural routing.

But the remedy is **targeted anti-evasion rules** (courts already scrutinize government-sponsored "initiatives"), not a permanent supermajority requirement that handicaps every authentic grassroots effort too. And Prop 43 doesn't lower anyone's taxes — it only removes one of the last revenue valves in a state whose local tax system Prop 13 already made the most constrained in the country.

**NO.**

# Vote **NO** on Proposition 43

## What it actually is
Prop 43 (ACA 22, Res. Ch. 132, Statutes of 2026) adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution — the article created by Prop 13. Effective **January 1, 2027**, it does two things:

1. **(a)** Any local **special tax** (money earmarked for a specific purpose) proposed by citizen initiative must now win **two-thirds** instead of a simple majority — reversing the *Upland* (2017) line of appellate rulings (SF Prop C 2020, Fresno 2020, *HJTA v. SF* 2021).
2. **(b)** Permanently **bans** local governments *and voters acting by initiative* from imposing **ad valorem (value-based) property taxes**, except as Art. XIII D allows.

It was placed on the ballot June 25, 2026 (Assembly 68–2, Senate 35–1) as a last-minute trade: the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its far more damaging "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13," which would have *retroactively voided* existing taxes and capped transfer taxes (LAO: up to ~$2B/year in local losses), and the Legislature pulled ACA 13 (a "poison pill" requiring supermajority measures to pass by supermajority).

## Why NO

**1. It's a permanent, unfixable restriction on majority rule.** This is a constitutional amendment, so the Legislature can never repair it — only voters can, and Prop 43 makes it harder for voters to act. It writes into the constitution that ~34% of voters can defeat what ~66% want, and it targets specifically the *initiative power*, the one tool designed for when elected officials won't act. Article XIII C expressly preserves the people's reserved power over local taxes; Prop 43 overrides Article II's initiative power "notwithstanding" language.

**2. There's an undisclosed provision.** Subdivision (b) — the ban on voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes — appears **nowhere** in the official title and summary, **nowhere** in the Legislative Analyst's analysis, and in **neither** ballot argument. It would forever foreclose a citizen initiative for a value-based property tax (e.g., a split-roll style commercial property reform). You're being asked to amend the constitution on the basis of materials that describe only half of it.

**3. It's backwards on accountability.** After Prop 43, *unrestricted* general taxes still pass by simple majority, while *dedicated, earmarked* special taxes — the more transparent, more accountable kind voters usually prefer — need two-thirds. It pushes communities toward less-accountable revenue. Even the **Mercury News/East Bay Times**, which endorsed YES, conceded the resulting structure is "backwards" and that real reform must be holistic. The Santa Cruz Sentinel board was divided and recommended NO for exactly that reason.

**4. Terrible timing and real casualties.** It kicks in Jan 1, 2027 — the same date California begins absorbing roughly **$30B/year in federal Medi-Cal cuts** under H.R. 1 — while local governments face wildfire, housing, and infrastructure costs. Measures that won majority support and would have died under this rule:

| Measure | Vote | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| LA Measure ULA (2022) | 57.8% | Affordable housing/homelessness ($1.4B raised) |
| SF Prop C (2018) | 61.3% | Homelessness services |
| SF Prop G (2018) | 60.8% | SFUSD teacher pay |
| Sonoma Measure H (2024) | ~62% | Fire, wildfire, EMS |
| Alameda Measure B (2025) | 64.7% | Washington Hospital parcel tax |
| Santa Clara Open Space Measure D (2026) | 55% | Wildfire/flood prevention, open space |
| Fresno Measure P (2018) | 52.2% | Parks (~$37.5M/yr) |
| Madera Measure T (2024) | 52% | Transportation |

Berkeley's city analysis lists comparable dedicated-revenue streams of $15M–$1.2B annually per city. It also blocks *renewals and increases* of expiring taxes.

**5. Follow the money and the misleading arguments.** The Yes side raised ~$14–15M, including **$9.87M from the California Business Roundtable Issues PAC** (top donors include Peter Thiel) and $1M each from Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett. The whole effort originated in the real estate industry's campaign against LA's mansion tax. The official YES argument also oversells: "2,000 new taxes" mostly weren't citizen-initiated special taxes (the only kind affected); "transfer taxes as high as 6%" are **not** capped by Prop 43 (that was the withdrawn initiative); and "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" is **already law** for special taxes. The No campaign's "$3 billion a year" claim is likewise not an LAO figure — the LAO says the impact is *unknown*.

**6. The near-unanimous legislative vote is not an endorsement.** The YES rebuttal touts it, but the author, **Assemblymember Buffy Wicks**, said days later she is "adamantly opposed" — she wrote it only to kill the retroactive measure. **Gov. Newsom**, who brokered the deal, now calls it "a dangerous corporate power grab." The CA Democratic Party, Becerra, LWV California, League of California Cities, CSAC, California Special Districts Assn., SPUR, ACLU SoCal, CA Professional Firefighters, CTA/CFT, SEIU Nurse Alliance, Cal School Employees Assn., and cities of Berkeley, West Hollywood and San José all oppose. Supporting: HJTA, CalTax, CA Business Roundtable, CA Small Business Assn., Reform California, CA GOP, and editorial boards of the Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, and Southern California News Group. Polling has it losing: PPIC (Oct) **42% yes / 55% no**; IGS–LA Times (Oct) **36% / 46%**.

**7. The courts already flagged this agenda.** In *Legislature v. Weber* (2024), the California Supreme Court **unanimously** removed the same sponsors' broader 2024 measure from the ballot as an invalid constitutional *revision*, citing its "far-reaching changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained." Prop 43 is a scaled-down attempt at the same project.

## The strongest case for YES — and why it doesn't win
The genuine problem is **sham citizen initiatives**: officials and interested parties route their own tax proposals through petition drives purely to halve the passage bar (SF supervisors' 2018 commercial rent tax at 50.8%; the San Diego hotel tax upheld at 65.2% after officials declared it failed; 2026's Measure RTM funded by transit unions/contractors instead of MTC; Oakland Measure E; the Fresno County fight where AB 1923 forced a disputed initiative onto the ballot). Consistency also has real value — identical taxes shouldn't face different thresholds based on procedural routing.

But the remedy is **targeted anti-evasion rules** (courts already scrutinize government-sponsored "initiatives"), not a permanent supermajority requirement that handicaps every authentic grassroots effort too. And Prop 43 doesn't lower anyone's taxes — it only removes one of the last revenue valves in a state whose local tax system Prop 13 already made the most constrained in the country.

**NO.**

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
PROPOSAL
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.

organizations governed by a board whose responsibility
is to ensure that the clinic meets its missions as a
safety-net health care provider and nonprofit public
benefit corporation subject to state and federal tax
exemptions.
(c) Clinic boards have significant responsibility and
exercise a great deal of authority in decisions on both
organization design and compensation, including that
of the Chief Executive Officer and other executives.
(d) Though existing state law requires nonprofit boards
of directors to review and approve Chief Executive
Officer and Chief Financial Officer compensation to
ensure that it is just and reasonable, many clinics pay
excessive shares of their revenue towards executive
compensation, resulting in underinvestment in core
patient services.

reasonable minimum standard of mission-directed
spending as a proportion of total revenue to ensure
clinic patient service delivery and workforce stability is
prioritized over management and overhead spending.

43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT
California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.
We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Proposition 13 was designed to make it harder to raise taxes, but court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved. Californians are paying billions in new or higher taxes they would not have to pay if it weren’t for these loopholes. Prop. 43 closes these loopholes and restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO RAISE YOUR TAXES
Local governments have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade, including higher sales, property and utility taxes-using the loopholes courts created in Prop. 13 to impose some of the most costly and damaging tax increases Californians face today.
These new and higher taxes make everything we buy or use more expensive, from food and gas to utilities and housing.
Prop. 43 guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes and restores the two-thirds vote for special local taxes.
PROP. 43 PROTECTS HOMEOWNERS FROM COSTLY NEW REAL ESTATE TAXES
California already has some of the highest housing costs in America, yet special interests are using court-created loopholes to add new taxes on the sale of homes, apartments and other real estate.
Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%. For California’s median-priced home of $900,000, that would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house. Those costs steal homeowners’ equity, raise apartment rents, and make building new housing more expensive.
Prop. 43 makes it much harder for special interests to impose these costly taxes on homeowners, renters, and small businesses.
PROP. 43 STOPS THE BAIT-AND-SWITCH TAX TRICKS
Politicians and special interests promise new taxes will fund schools, roads, and public safety-only to divert the money elsewhere and frustrate the will of voters. Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved and restores the broad voter support required before politicians and special interests impose earmarked tax measures.
If taxpayers are asked to pay more, they deserve the right to vote and the confidence their money will be spent as promised.
PROP. 43 PUTS VOTERS BACK IN CHARGE
Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.
Vote YES on Prop. 43:
• Affirms the voters’ right to vote on all new or higher local taxes. • Restores the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. • Protects Proposition 13 and closes court-created loopholes. • Makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes. • Protects homeowners, renters, and small businesses from new real estate taxes. • Strengthens accountability for how taxpayer dollars are spent.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Robert Rivinius , President
Family Business Association of California
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
We all want relief from California’s high cost of living. But Proposition 43 doesn’t cut your taxes a penny. It attacks something far more valuable: the power of your vote.
PROP. 43 WEAKENS YOUR VOTE.
Today, when local voters decide how to fund their communities, the majority rules. Prop. 43 throws that out, letting just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Under Prop. 43, a NO vote counts twice as much as a YES. That isn’t fair, and it isn’t democracy.
PROP. 43 DEEPENS THE HOUSING CRISIS.
Across California, communities vote to build affordable homes for working families, seniors, and veterans. They are helping renters stay housed and move people off the streets. Prop. 43 hands a small minority the power to block those solutions, even when a clear majority of your neighbors support them.
PROP. 43 TIES YOUR COMMUNITY’S HANDS.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund the critical local services your community counts on: staffing fire stations and 911 response, preparing neighborhoods for wildfire, repairing crumbling roads, keeping schools, parks, and libraries open, and protecting local hospitals and clinics as Washington cuts healthcare funding. When funding is blocked, help arrives slower, classrooms grow more crowded, and communities are left less safe.
KEEP THE POWER WHERE IT BELONGS-WITH YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBORS.
That’s why teachers, nurses, firefighters, and housing advocates all oppose Prop. 43.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Nick Lapis , Director of Advocacy
Californians Against Waste
Bill Barnes , Director of Campaigns & Community
Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California
Steve Frisch , President
Sierra Business Council
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 43
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund critical services like police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff our local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts. Prop. 43 undermines the voice of voters and the majority vote by letting just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions-and it makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FUND FIRE AND POLICE SERVICES.
Local police and firefighters can’t rely on Sacramento or Washington politicians. These services are funded at the local level. Prop. 43 wants to make it harder for local voters to direct new funding to services like police and fire. Without adequate funding, 911 response times are slower, fire stations sit understaffed, and families wait longer for help when every second counts. When a house fire breaks out-or a wildfire threatens our neighborhoods-that local funding is what protects us. Prop. 43 would let a small minority of voters block it. Even if 66% of voters say yes, Prop. 43 would prevent us from funding desperately needed local services.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FIX ROADS, FUND SCHOOLS, AND PROTECT HEALTHCARE.
Across California, local voters have come together to repair crumbling roads and improve transportation, to fund their neighborhood schools, and to protect local hospitals and healthcare-especially as Washington cuts federal health funding. These are decisions communities make for themselves, by majority vote. Instead, Prop. 43 hands a small group of voters the power to veto those solutions, even when the majority supports them.
PROP. 43 EMPOWERS 33.4% OF VOTERS OVER THE WILL OF THE MAJORITY.
In America, we believe in one person, one vote-and the majority wins. Prop. 43 throws that out. It empowers just over one-third of voters to block what nearly 67% want. It puts the out-voted minority in charge-even if they are extremists. It makes their NO vote count twice as much as a YES vote.
CORPORATE DONORS BENEFIT. NOT TAXPAYERS.
Under Prop. 43, corporate donors who spend big in elections will benefit most. Right now, voters can hold these corporations and developers accountable at the ballot box, and make them pay their fair share for local needs. Prop. 43 is designed to take that power away-to protect the powerful few, at everyone else’s expense.
That’s why these organizations are asking you to vote NO on Prop. 43:
• California Professional Firefighters • Californians Against Waste • California Federation of Teachers • California School Employees Association • Communities for a Better Environment • AAPI Force • Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California • Nurses Alliance of SEIU California • Sierra Business Council
Vote NO to protect your vote and majority rule. Keep the power where it belongs-with you and your neighbors.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Harkins , Executive Director
Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
Adam Weinberger , President
California School Employees Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43 TO RESTORE TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Californians already pay high taxes. But instead of prioritizing funding for critical services like police and fire, local politicians waste your money on their pet projects- then demand tax increases, claiming the need to fund the most important priorities.
The state Constitution requires a two-thirds vote for taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, but recent court decisions created a loophole that allowed special taxes to pass with fewer votes. Now Californians are paying billions in taxes they should not have had to pay.
Prop. 43 RESTORES the longstanding two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes, protecting homeowners, renters, and small businesses from costly new sales and parcel taxes, taxes on electricity and gas, and real estate taxes.
Prop. 43 GUARANTEES taxpayers the right to vote on new or higher local taxes and requires governments to spend taxpayer dollars for the specific purposes voters approved-preventing bait-and-switch schemes that make our sky-high cost of living even worse.
Over the last decade, local governments have imposed 2,000 new or higher taxes. Prop. 43 CLOSES LOOPHOLES used to pass some of the most damaging tax increases, restores the protections voters originally approved under Proposition 13, and makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes without broad voter support.
The Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot sends a clear message: activist courts exceeded voters’ intent by creating loopholes that weakened Proposition 13’s protections.
Restore your right to vote on ALL local taxes.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association

Key finding: The actual constitutional text (Sec. 4.5 of Article XIII A) does MORE than what the title and summary describes. Specifically:

(a) Beginning January 1, 2027, no local government, INCLUDING the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax... unless approved by two-thirds vote.

(b) Notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D.

This (b) provision is a complete BAN on new voter-initiated ad valorem (property value-based) real estate taxes — not just a two-thirds requirement. Wait, is it a ban? "no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D."

Article XIII D, Section 3(a)(1) — Let me recall. Article XIII D (Prop 218) Section 3 requires property-related taxes/fees. Actually, Article XIII D Section 3(a) says: "No fee or charge may be imposed by any agency upon a parcel or a person as an incident of property ownership..." That's about assessments. Hmm.

Actually let me check: Article XIII D, Section 3(a): "No fee or charge may be imposed by any agency upon a parcel or a person as an incident of property ownership other than: (1) A tax, special assessment, or property-related fee or charge, imposed in accordance with Sections 1, 2, and 4 of this article..." Hmm. Let me look at the actual text.

Actually Article XIII D Sec 3(a)(1) says: "A tax, special assessment, or property-related fee or charge, imposed in accordance with Sections 1, 2, and 4 of this article, or the procedures set forth in Section 4 of Article XIII C, may be imposed."

Hmm, so exception (1) allows property-related taxes imposed in accordance with Article XIII C procedures (which include the two-thirds vote for special taxes). Let me actually read the text of Article XIII D Section 3.

So (b) may be interpreted as: local governments/electorate may not impose ad valorem taxes on real property, EXCEPT as provided in Art XIII D §3(a)(1) — i.e., taxes imposed per Art XIII C (which requires two-thirds for special taxes). This is ambiguous and has been flagged by critics. Actually the intent seems to be: no more split-roll type property taxes, no more ad valorem transfer taxes... Let me look for legal analysis.

This is an important detail: the LAO analysis in the voter guide ONLY describes the two-thirds requirement for special tax initiatives, but the constitutional text also has a provision banning local ad valorem real property taxes via initiative. The official title/summary does not mention it either. That's a significant omission — and one that has been criticized.

Let me research ACA 22's legislative history, and news coverage about the property tax initiative prohibition.

Let me also research: the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, who funded/supports it; the coalition against. And polling.

Let me search.
