Guest Commentary written by Sandra Lowe Sandra Lowe is a member of the Sonoma City Council and a longtime political consultant. Sometimes things that sound simple are not. Let’s take Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/). Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments’ decisions: majority rule. Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority. Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected. In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H (https://sonomacounty.gov/administrative-support-and-fiscal-services/county-executives-office/strategic-initiatives/fire-services-project/measure-h) in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee. Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote (https://ballotpedia.org/Sonoma_County,_California,_Measure_H,_Fire_Prevention_and_Disaster_Response_Sales_Tax_Measure_(March_2024)). READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) California courts muddied tax rules set by voters. Proposition 43 cleans up their mistake (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders. No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent. Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions. The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding (https://health.alamedacountyca.gov/program/measures-a-c-and-w/) and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation (https://www.openspaceauthority.org/whats-new/press-release-measure-d). Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime. Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let’s not go backward. Read more from CalMatters Text Get breaking news on your phone. California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

# Proposition 43
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
### Fiscal Effects

CONSENT ITEM
September 29, 2026
TO: Honorable Berkeley City City Councilmembers
FROM: Mayor Adena Ishii (Author), Councilmember Lunaparra (Co-Sponsor),
Councilmember Blackaby (Co-Sponsor), Councilmember Tregub (Co-Sponsor)
SUBJECT: Recommendation to Oppose Proposition 43, Limits Voter’s Ability to Raise
Revenues for Local Government Services
RECOMMENDATION
Berkeley City Council adopt a resolution opposing Proposition 43, a constitutional amendment
on the November 2026 statewide ballot to limit voter's ability to raise revenues for local
government services.
Summary:
Proposition 43 is a legislatively proposed constitutional amendment (ACA 22) that would change
the voter-approval requirements for local special taxes and will appear before voters at the
November 3, 2026, statewide general election.
Beginning January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would require all local special taxes to receive
approval from two-thirds of the voters voting on the tax, regardless of whether the measure is
placed on the ballot by a local governing body or through the local initiative process.
The measure would also prohibit a local government, including its electorate acting through the
initiative power, from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property except as permitted under
existing constitutional provisions.
Ballot Description:
Proposition 43 would add Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution and make
the following changes to local taxation authority:
Two-Thirds Requirement for All Local Special Taxes
Beginning January 1, 2027, a local government, including the electorate of a local
government exercising the initiative power, could not impose, extend, or increase a
special tax unless the tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
Local government-sponsored special taxes are already subject to two-thirds voter
approval under Article XIII C. Proposition 43 would extend that same threshold to
special taxes proposed through the voter initiative process, reversing the current judicial
interpretation that permits those measures to pass with a simple majority.
Ad Valorem Property Tax Limitation
Proposition 43 would prohibit a local government, including its electorate acting through
the initiative power, from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property except as
authorized by paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D of the
California Constitution. This provision clarifies that the existing constitutional limitation
applies to both local governing bodies and local voters acting by initiative.
Prospective Application
The measure would operate prospectively, applying to voter-proposed ballot measures
approved after January 1, 2027.
BACKGROUND:
Proposition 13 and Local Tax Approval Requirements
California's modern local tax framework largely stems from Proposition 131, approved by voters
in 1978. Proposition 13 limited property tax rates and established voter approval requirements
for local taxes. Specifically, it capped the general ad valorem property tax rate at 1 percent of
assessed value, limited annual increases in assessed value, and required two-thirds voter approval
for cities, counties, and special districts to impose special taxes.
Proposition 218, approved by voters in 1996, added Articles XIII C and XIII D to the California
Constitution. Under Article XIII C, local governments may not impose, extend, or increase a
special tax without approval by two-thirds of voters. A special tax is defined as any tax imposed
for a specific purpose rather than for general governmental use.
Article XIII C also classifies local taxes as either general or special. General taxes used for
general governmental purposes generally require majority voter approval. When proposed by a
local governing body, a general tax must generally appear on the ballot at a regularly scheduled
general election for members of that governing body, unless an emergency is declared by a
unanimous vote.
Article XIII C also expressly preserves the voters' initiative power to reduce or repeal local taxes,
assessments, fees, and charges. More broadly, Article II of the California Constitution reserves
the initiative power to the people, and courts have traditionally construed that power broadly.
Court Decisions Affecting Initiative Taxes
Recent court decisions have interpreted these constitutional provisions differently when taxes are
proposed through the citizen initiative process rather than by a local government.
California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland
California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017) 3 Cal.5th 924 arose from a local
initiative to repeal the city's ban on medical marijuana dispensaries, and impose an
annual $75,000 licensing and inspection charge. The City of Upland concluded that
1 California Proposition 43, Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and
Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment (2026) - Ballotpedia
because the charge exceeded estimated regulatory costs, it would operate as a general tax
and had to appear at a regularly scheduled general election rather than the special election
requested by the proponents.
The California Supreme Court held that Article XIII C's election-timing requirement
applied to taxes imposed by a 'local government' and did not clearly restrict voters acting
through the initiative power. The requirement therefore did not apply to the voter-
sponsored initiative. Upland addressed election timing for a voter-initiated general tax,
not the approval threshold for a voter-initiated special tax.
San Francisco Proposition C and the Current Majority Threshold
Following Upland, the Court of Appeal in City and County of San Francisco v. All
Persons Interested in the Matter of Proposition C (2020) 51 Cal.App.5th 703 held that a
voter-initiated local special tax may be approved by a simple majority rather than two-
thirds of voters. The California Supreme Court declined review. Subsequent appellate
decisions followed the same approach, allowing several voter-initiated local special taxes
to take effect with majority approval.
Under current law, the approval threshold for a local special tax therefore depends on how the
measure reaches the ballot. A governing-body-sponsored special tax requires two-thirds voter
approval, while a voter-initiated special tax may pass with a majority. Proposition 43 would
eliminate that distinction by applying the two-thirds threshold to both.
ACA 13 (Ward)
In 2023, the League of California Cities supported ACA 13 a constitutional amendment dealing
with voter thresholds. The measure would have required any state or local initiative measure to
conform with any increased voter threshold that it seeks to impose on future ballot measures. For
example, if a measure looks to increase the voter threshold of general tax measures from a
simple majority (50% +1) to a supermajority (2/3), the measure would be required to pass by that
same supermajority.
The measure would have also preserved the right of local governments to place advisory
questions on the ballot to ask voters their opinion on the issue.
ACA 13 also stated that the provisions of this constitutional amendment apply to all statewide
initiative measures submitted to voters on or after January 1, 2024. It contained intent language
stating that the provisions of this measure are not intended to reverse or invalidate provisions of
the California Constitution in effect before January 1, 2024, including the provisions of
Proposition 13 of 1978.
ACA 13 was originally scheduled to be on the March 2024 ballot, but was subsequently moved
to the November 2024 ballot, and then again to the November 2026 ballot.
The 2026 Ballot Agreement
ACA 22, the legislation to place Proposition 43 on the November ballot, is the product of an
agreement between state leaders and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA). In
exchange for the Legislature passing ACA 22 and removing ACA 13 from the November ballot,
HJTA withdrew its Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Initiative 25-
0006A1). The proposal included a two-thirds requirement for all local special taxes, restrictions
on real property transfer taxes, and the invalidation of certain existing taxes. The League of
California Cities opposed the measure based on its effects on existing voter-approved revenues,
local taxation authority, and essential local services.
Proposition 43 would operate prospectively and would not repeal or reduce existing real property
transfer taxes, invalidate existing voter-approved special taxes, limit documentary transfer tax
rates, or create a deadline for local governments to eliminate existing taxes. The result is a new
constitutional restriction on future local revenue measures by requiring two-thirds approval for
voter-initiated special taxes that may pass by majority vote under current law.
Proposition 43 Fiscal Impact:
Proposition 43 would not directly reduce or eliminate existing city revenues. Current real
property transfer taxes, parcel taxes, and other voter-initiated special taxes would remain in
effect. Its fiscal effects would instead arise when future voter-initiated special taxes receive
majority support but fall short of the new two-thirds threshold.
The statewide amount of foregone revenue cannot be reliably estimated because it would depend
on the number, structure, tax base, and election results of future local measures.
Existing voter-initiated special taxes illustrate the potential scale of revenue that could be
affected if comparable measures are proposed after January 1, 2027. Examples of existing taxes
that passed with less than two-thirds support include:
● Los Angeles Measure ULA: approximately $655 million to $1.2 billion annually.
● Santa Monica Measure GS: approximately $54 million annually.
● Oakland Measure AA: approximately $30 million to $36 million annually.
● Berkeley Measure FF: approximately $15 million annually.
Proposition 43 would not invalidate or reduce revenue from these existing measures. However, a
future measure with the same level of voter support would not take effect unless it received two-
thirds approval. These examples are therefore illustrative of the type and magnitude of future
locally dedicated revenue that could be foregone, not an estimate of an immediate revenue loss
under the measure
Additionally, Proposition 43 may also influence how future revenue measures are structured.
Communities may favor general taxes, which remain subject to majority approval, over special
taxes dedicated to specific purposes. Although this may preserve a path to revenue, it would
prevent voters from legally restricting the funds to the program identified in the measure and
could place additional demands on a city's general fund.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS:
Opposing Proposition 43 has no financial implications for the City of Berkeley.

Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16

# Vote **NO** on Proposition 43

## What it actually is
Prop 43 (ACA 22, Res. Ch. 132, Statutes of 2026) adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution — the article created by Prop 13. Effective **January 1, 2027**, it does two things:

1. **(a)** Any local **special tax** (money earmarked for a specific purpose) proposed by citizen initiative must now win **two-thirds** instead of a simple majority — reversing the *Upland* (2017) line of appellate rulings (SF Prop C 2020, Fresno 2020, *HJTA v. SF* 2021).
2. **(b)** Permanently **bans** local governments *and voters acting by initiative* from imposing **ad valorem (value-based) property taxes**, except as Art. XIII D allows.

It was placed on the ballot June 25, 2026 (Assembly 68–2, Senate 35–1) as a last-minute trade: the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its far more damaging "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13," which would have *retroactively voided* existing taxes and capped transfer taxes (LAO: up to ~$2B/year in local losses), and the Legislature pulled ACA 13 (a "poison pill" requiring supermajority measures to pass by supermajority).

## Why NO

**1. It's a permanent, unfixable restriction on majority rule.** This is a constitutional amendment, so the Legislature can never repair it — only voters can, and Prop 43 makes it harder for voters to act. It writes into the constitution that ~34% of voters can defeat what ~66% want, and it targets specifically the *initiative power*, the one tool designed for when elected officials won't act. Article XIII C expressly preserves the people's reserved power over local taxes; Prop 43 overrides Article II's initiative power "notwithstanding" language.

**2. There's an undisclosed provision.** Subdivision (b) — the ban on voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes — appears **nowhere** in the official title and summary, **nowhere** in the Legislative Analyst's analysis, and in **neither** ballot argument. It would forever foreclose a citizen initiative for a value-based property tax (e.g., a split-roll style commercial property reform). You're being asked to amend the constitution on the basis of materials that describe only half of it.

**3. It's backwards on accountability.** After Prop 43, *unrestricted* general taxes still pass by simple majority, while *dedicated, earmarked* special taxes — the more transparent, more accountable kind voters usually prefer — need two-thirds. It pushes communities toward less-accountable revenue. Even the **Mercury News/East Bay Times**, which endorsed YES, conceded the resulting structure is "backwards" and that real reform must be holistic. The Santa Cruz Sentinel board was divided and recommended NO for exactly that reason.

**4. Terrible timing and real casualties.** It kicks in Jan 1, 2027 — the same date California begins absorbing roughly **$30B/year in federal Medi-Cal cuts** under H.R. 1 — while local governments face wildfire, housing, and infrastructure costs. Measures that won majority support and would have died under this rule:

| Measure | Vote | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| LA Measure ULA (2022) | 57.8% | Affordable housing/homelessness ($1.4B raised) |
| SF Prop C (2018) | 61.3% | Homelessness services |
| SF Prop G (2018) | 60.8% | SFUSD teacher pay |
| Sonoma Measure H (2024) | ~62% | Fire, wildfire, EMS |
| Alameda Measure B (2025) | 64.7% | Washington Hospital parcel tax |
| Santa Clara Open Space Measure D (2026) | 55% | Wildfire/flood prevention, open space |

| Madera Measure T (2024) | 52% | Transportation |

Berkeley's city analysis lists comparable dedicated-revenue streams of $15M–$1.2B annually per city. It also blocks *renewals and increases* of expiring taxes.

**5. Follow the money and the misleading arguments.** The Yes side raised ~$14–15M, including **$9.87M from the California Business Roundtable Issues PAC** (top donors include Peter Thiel) and $1M each from Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett. The whole effort originated in the real estate industry's campaign against LA's mansion tax. The official YES argument also oversells: "2,000 new taxes" mostly weren't citizen-initiated special taxes (the only kind affected); "transfer taxes as high as 6%" are **not** capped by Prop 43 (that was the withdrawn initiative); and "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" is **already law** for special taxes. The No campaign's "$3 billion a year" claim is likewise not an LAO figure — the LAO says the impact is *unknown*.

**6. The near-unanimous legislative vote is not an endorsement.** The YES rebuttal touts it, but the author, **Assemblymember Buffy Wicks**, said days later she is "adamantly opposed" — she wrote it only to kill the retroactive measure. **Gov. Newsom**, who brokered the deal, now calls it "a dangerous corporate power grab." The CA Democratic Party, Becerra, LWV California, League of California Cities, CSAC, California Special Districts Assn., SPUR, ACLU SoCal, CA Professional Firefighters, CTA/CFT, SEIU Nurse Alliance, Cal School Employees Assn., and cities of Berkeley, West Hollywood and San José all oppose. Supporting: HJTA, CalTax, CA Business Roundtable, CA Small Business Assn., Reform California, CA GOP, and editorial boards of the Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, and Southern California News Group. Polling has it losing: PPIC (Oct) **42% yes / 55% no**; IGS–LA Times (Oct) **36% / 46%**.

**7. The courts already flagged this agenda.** In *Legislature v. Weber* (2024), the California Supreme Court **unanimously** removed the same sponsors' broader 2024 measure from the ballot as an invalid constitutional *revision*, citing its "far-reaching changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained." Prop 43 is a scaled-down attempt at the same project.

## The strongest case for YES — and why it doesn't win
The genuine problem is **sham citizen initiatives**: officials and interested parties route their own tax proposals through petition drives purely to halve the passage bar (SF supervisors' 2018 commercial rent tax at 50.8%; the San Diego hotel tax upheld at 65.2% after officials declared it failed; 2026's Measure RTM funded by transit unions/contractors instead of MTC; Oakland Measure E; the Fresno County fight where AB 1923 forced a disputed initiative onto the ballot). Consistency also has real value — identical taxes shouldn't face different thresholds based on procedural routing.

But the remedy is **targeted anti-evasion rules** (courts already scrutinize government-sponsored "initiatives"), not a permanent supermajority requirement that handicaps every authentic grassroots effort too. And Prop 43 doesn't lower anyone's taxes — it only removes one of the last revenue valves in a state whose local tax system Prop 13 already made the most constrained in the country.

**NO.**
